questions.explanation: Under-capitalisation means operating with small capital, so each naira earns a high return on investment, though the firm may be stretched. Option B is the opposite case, over-capitalisation, and Option C describes negative working capital rather than under-capitalisation.

questions.question: Agege Foods Plc keeps huge balances of idle cash and stock far above what its operations need, and its return on investment has become very small. This situation is best described as:
questions.explanation: Over-capitalisation means huge capital giving a small return on investment, exactly what idle cash and excess stock produce. Option D is the opposite (small capital, high return), Option A uses minimal current assets and short-term funds, and Option C means expanding sales too fast on too little capital.

questions.question: The working capital cycle is best defined as:

options.a: The period over which a fixed asset is depreciated
options.b: The time between placing an order with a supplier and receiving the goods
options.c: The number of times stock is replaced in a year
options.d: The total length of time required to convert cash into raw materials, work in progress, finished goods and debtors, and back into cash

questions.explanation: The working capital cycle is the total time needed to go from cash back to cash through raw inputs, work in progress, finished goods and debtors. Option C is stock turnover, Option B is the lead time used in setting the reorder level, and Option A has nothing to do with working capital.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows the working capital cycle of a manufacturing company?

options.a: Cash - raw materials - work in progress - finished goods - debtors - cash
options.b: Cash - finished goods - raw materials - work in progress - debtors - cash
options.c: Cash - debtors - finished goods - work in progress - raw materials - cash
options.d: Cash - raw materials - finished goods - work in progress - creditors - cash

questions.explanation: Cash buys raw inputs (raw stock), which become work in progress and then finished goods; these are sold on credit to create debtors, who finally pay cash. Option C runs the cycle backwards, Option B puts finished goods before production, and Option D swaps the production stages and replaces debtors with creditors.

questions.question: In the working capital cycle, which event comes immediately after the conversion of work in progress into finished goods?

options.a: Conversion of raw materials to work in progress
options.b: Conversion of finished goods to debtors through credit sales
options.c: Conversion of cash to raw materials

questions.explanation: Once goods are finished they are sold on credit, turning them into debtors; only after that do debtors pay cash. Option C is the first stage and Option A is the second, and Option D is the final stage that comes after debtors are created.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a stage of the working capital cycle?

options.a: Conversion of fixed assets to cash
options.b: Conversion of cash to raw materials
options.c: Conversion of finished goods to debtors

questions.explanation: The cycle involves only current items: cash, raw inputs, work in progress, finished goods and debtors. Selling fixed assets is a long-term investment decision, not part of the day-to-day cycle.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed among the factors affecting the working capital of a company?

options.a: Inflation rate prevailing in the economy
options.c: Nominal value of the company's ordinary shares

questions.explanation: The nominal (par) value of shares is an accounting label on equity and does not change how much stock, debtors or cash a firm needs. The production cycle, inflation and business fluctuations all directly change the working capital a company must hold.

questions.question: Which of the following is a factor affecting the working capital of a company?

options.b: Number of directors on the board
options.c: Date of incorporation of the company
options.d: Dividend policy adopted by the company

questions.explanation: Dividend policy affects working capital because paying out cash dividends drains the cash available for day-to-day operations. The number of directors, date of incorporation and registered office have no direct effect on the level of current assets.

questions.question: A Lagos furniture maker takes four months to turn timber into finished wardrobes, while a nearby bakery turns flour into bread in one day. The furniture maker needs far more working capital mainly because of its:
questions.explanation: A longer production cycle keeps cash tied up in raw inputs and work in progress for longer, so more working capital is needed. Dividend policy, availability of credit and inflation can also affect working capital, but the difference described here comes from the length of production.

questions.question: Eko Distributors decides to give customers 90 days to pay instead of 30 days. Which factor affecting working capital is at work, and what is its likely effect?

options.a: Size of the business; working capital is unaffected
options.b: Operating efficiency; working capital requirement falls
options.c: Credit policy; working capital requirement falls as debtors decrease
options.d: Credit policy; working capital requirement rises as debtors increase

questions.explanation: The credit policy adopted by a company is a factor affecting working capital. Longer credit terms mean customers pay later, so debtors build up and more working capital is tied up. Option C gets the direction wrong, and the other options name the wrong factor.

questions.question: In stock management, the term 'stock' refers to:

options.d: Raw materials, work in progress and finished goods

questions.explanation: Stock (inventory) covers raw inputs, work in progress and finished goods. Option C refers to stock in the sense of shares, which is a different meaning of the word, and the remaining options are other current assets.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the tasks involved in the management of stock?

options.b: Setting the maximum and minimum levels of stock

questions.explanation: Stock management involves setting the reorder level, the re-order quantity, and the maximum and minimum stock levels, all aimed at minimising total stock cost in production. The dividend payout ratio is a long-term finance decision.

questions.question: The re-order quantity that minimises the total of stock carrying cost and stock ordering cost is also known as the:
questions.explanation: The re-order quantity that minimises carrying plus ordering cost is the optimal re-order quantity or economic order quantity (EOQ). Option D is the stock level that triggers an order, not the quantity ordered, Option A is a buffer against stock-outs, and Option B is an upper control limit.

questions.question: Where D is annual demand, OC is the cost per order and CC is the annual carrying cost per unit, the total annual carrying cost at order quantity Q* is:
questions.explanation: Average stock is half the order quantity, so total carrying cost = (Q* / 2) x CC. Option B is the total ordering cost, Option D forgets that only half the order is held on average, and Option C charges carrying cost on the whole year's demand.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the basic economic order quantity model?

options.a: Quantity discounts are available for bulk purchases
options.c: Annual demand and cost per order are constant
options.d: Purchase price per unit is known with certainty

questions.explanation: The basic EOQ model assumes no discount is allowed, so quantity discounts break its assumptions. It also assumes no stock-outs, a known price per unit, and constant annual demand, ordering cost and carrying cost.

questions.question: Which of the following is an assumption underlying the economic order quantity model?

options.a: Stock-outs are allowed if they reduce costs
options.d: Ordering cost rises with every order placed

questions.explanation: The EOQ model assumes annual carrying cost is constant, along with constant demand and cost per order, no discounts and no stock-outs. The other options contradict those assumptions.

questions.question: Which costs does the economic order quantity seek to minimise?
questions.explanation: EOQ balances ordering cost against carrying cost; these two make up the controllable cost. Total purchase cost (price x annual demand) is the same whatever order size is chosen, so options that include it are wrong.

questions.question: At the economic order quantity, which relationship always holds in the basic EOQ model?

options.a: Total ordering cost equals total purchase cost
options.c: Number of orders equals the order quantity
options.d: Total ordering cost equals total carrying cost

questions.explanation: At the optimum the two controllable costs are equal, which gives a quick check on any EOQ answer. Option A confuses ordering with purchase cost, Option B would only happen if no stock were ever held, and Option C is a coincidence that happens only for particular figures.

questions.question: If the annual carrying cost per unit rises while demand and ordering cost stay the same, the economic order quantity will:
questions.explanation: Carrying cost is in the denominator of EOQ = square root of (2 x D x OC / CC), so a higher carrying cost makes it cheaper to hold less stock and order more often, and the EOQ falls. Option D would follow from higher demand or ordering cost, not higher carrying cost.

questions.question: Safety (buffer) stock is best described as:

options.a: Goods received from suppliers but not yet paid for
options.b: The quantity ordered each time an order is placed
options.c: Extra stock held to protect against running out when usage or lead time is higher than expected
options.d: Stock that has become obsolete and must be written off

questions.explanation: Safety stock is a cushion kept above normal needs so that the firm does not run out during delays or unusual demand; it is added to the reorder level. Option B is the order quantity, while Option D and Option A describe obsolete stock and unpaid purchases.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the steps involved in cash management?
questions.explanation: Cash management involves cash budgeting, managing the cash book, determining the optimal cash balance, investing surplus funds and financing deficits. The economic order quantity belongs to stock management, not cash management.

questions.question: A cash budget is best defined as:

options.a: A statement of assets and liabilities at a point in time
options.b: A list of debtors arranged by how long they have owed
options.c: A statement of expected cash receipts and expected cash payments over a future period
options.d: A record of profit earned over the past year

questions.explanation: A cash budget shows the expected cash income and expected cash expenditure over a coming period, which may be daily, weekly, monthly or quarterly. Option A is a balance sheet, Option D is an income statement, and Option B is an age analysis of debtors.

questions.question: A Nigerian firm's cash budget shows a large surplus of cash expected next quarter. Which cash management step should follow?
questions.explanation: Investing the surplus fund is one of the steps of cash management; idle cash earns nothing, so a forecast surplus should be placed in suitable short-term investments. Option D applies when the budget shows a shortfall, and the other options are stock and debtors decisions.

questions.question: Debtors management is mainly concerned with:

options.a: How fast the company recovers cash from its debtors
options.b: How much stock the company holds
options.c: How quickly the company pays its suppliers
options.d: How the company raises long-term loans

questions.explanation: Debtors management is about how fast cash is recovered from customers who bought on credit, through good ledger records, credit policy and a recovery plan. Option C is creditors (payables) management and Option B is stock management.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the factors to consider for proper debtors management?

options.b: Adequate and updated ledger account statements

questions.explanation: Proper debtors management needs updated ledger statements, a sound credit policy, a recovery plan and proper recovery of cash from bad debtors. The reorder level is a stock management tool.

questions.question: In the credit terms '2/10 net 45', what does the 45 represent?

options.a: The number of days within which the discount can be taken
options.b: The maximum payment period in days
options.d: The interest rate charged on late payment

questions.explanation: In 2/10 net 45, the 45 is the maximum payment period: the full invoice must be paid within 45 days. The 10 is the discount period in days and the 2 is the percentage discount.

questions.question: A supplier sells on terms of '3/15 net 60'. What do the 3 and the 15 mean?

options.a: A 15% discount is available if payment is made within 3 days
options.b: Interest of 3% is charged on balances unpaid after 15 days
options.c: A 3% discount is available if payment is made within 15 days
options.d: Payment must be made in 3 instalments over 15 days

questions.explanation: The first figure is the percentage discount and the second is the number of days in which it can be claimed, so 3% is deducted if the buyer pays within 15 days; otherwise the full amount is due by day 60. Option A swaps the two figures.

questions.question: When calculating the cost of not taking a cash discount, which day count should be used if the question does not state one?

options.b: The number of days in the credit period

questions.explanation: The default is a 365-day year; 360 days is used only when a question explicitly says the company operates a 360-day year. The result is sensitive to this choice, so always read the question first. Option D and Option B are not standard day counts.

questions.question: Gross working capital refers to:

options.c: The total investment in current assets

questions.explanation: Gross working capital is the total of current assets. Option B is net working capital, the measure used in the standard definition of working capital, and Option D is capital employed.

questions.question: Permanent working capital is best described as:

options.a: Current assets needed only during seasonal peaks
options.b: The fixed assets of the business
options.c: Working capital financed entirely by trade creditors
options.d: The minimum level of current assets a firm needs at all times to carry on its operations

questions.explanation: Permanent working capital is the minimum level of current assets that never disappears while the business operates. Option A describes temporary (fluctuating) working capital, and Option B is a fixed asset, not working capital.

questions.question: Under an aggressive working capital financing policy, a firm:

options.a: Holds large cash balances financed by equity
options.b: Uses short-term funds to finance temporary current assets and part of its permanent assets
options.c: Matches the maturity of each source of finance to the life of the asset financed
options.d: Uses long-term funds to finance all permanent assets and all temporary current assets

questions.explanation: An aggressive policy relies heavily on cheap but risky short-term finance, using it even for part of the permanent assets. Option D is a conservative policy, Option C is the matching (hedging) approach, and Option A describes over-cautious liquidity rather than an aggressive policy.

questions.question: Which working capital financing policy uses long-term funds to finance all permanent assets and some or all of the temporary current assets, giving low risk but lower profitability?
questions.explanation: A conservative policy leans on long-term finance even for part of the seasonal needs, so the firm rarely faces refinancing pressure but pays more for its funds. Option A uses more short-term finance and Option B finances temporary assets only with short-term funds.

questions.question: Kwara Rice Mills Ltd keeps extra cash in its account in case a machine breaks down unexpectedly or a customer delays payment. Which motive for holding cash does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Holding cash as a cushion against unexpected events is the precautionary motive. Option A covers routine payments such as wages and suppliers, Option C is holding cash to take advantage of opportunities such as a fall in prices, and Option B relates to balances a bank requires.

questions.question: A Kano trader holds extra cash so she can buy large quantities of grain if prices fall sharply after harvest. This reflects the:
questions.explanation: Keeping cash ready to profit from favourable price movements is the speculative motive. Option D is cash for routine day-to-day payments, Option B is cash kept for emergencies, and Option C is not one of the motives for holding cash.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The concept of diversification in finance refers to:
questions.explanation: Diversification means spreading money across different investments so that a loss on one can be offset by gains on others, reducing overall risk. Option A, putting all funds in one asset, is the opposite and increases risk.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Systematic risk is:
questions.explanation: Systematic risk is market-wide risk, from factors such as recessions, inflation or interest rate changes, that affects all firms. Options A and D describe unsystematic risk, and C is wrong because diversification cannot remove systematic risk.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Unsystematic risk can be reduced by:
questions.explanation: Unsystematic risk is specific to individual firms, so holding many different assets lets losses on some be offset by gains on others. Option A increases this risk, and D avoids risk only by giving up any return.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of systematic risk?
questions.explanation: An economic downturn hits almost all firms at once, so it is a systematic (market) risk. Poor leadership (A), a faulty product (C) and a strike at one company (D) are firm-specific, unsystematic risks.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A portfolio is:
questions.explanation: A portfolio is a collection or combination of investments, such as shares and bonds, held by one investor. Option A confuses it with a set of financial statements, while C and D describe a cash management strategy and a tax plan, not a group of investments.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Market risk is also known as:
questions.explanation: Market risk is the risk that affects the whole market, for example from inflation or interest rate changes, and it is also called systematic risk. It cannot be removed by diversification, so options A and C (diversifiable or unsystematic risk) describe the opposite type. Credit risk (D) is the risk that a borrower fails to repay.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: An investment holding that consists of a minimum of two different securities, also described as a basket of investment, is called a:
questions.explanation: A portfolio is a combination of at least two different securities, which is why it is also called a basket of investment. Option A is the line drawn from the CAPM equation, Option C measures systematic risk, and Option B is a single riskless investment such as a treasury bill.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Portfolio theory is best described as:

options.a: The way a portfolio is selected with the aim of reducing or minimising the risk on that portfolio
options.b: The way a single security is priced so that its return equals the market return
options.c: The way a firm decides how much of its profit to pay out as dividends
options.d: The way an investor chooses the one security with the highest expected return

questions.explanation: Portfolio theory is about selecting a combination of securities so that the risk of the whole portfolio is reduced, eliminated or minimised. Option D describes putting everything into one high-return security, which ignores risk, while Option B is closer to the pricing idea in CAPM and Option C is dividend policy.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: In the expression PR = WxRx + WyRy, the terms Wx and Wy represent:

options.a: The standard deviation of each security
options.b: The expected return of each security
options.d: The proportion of each security in the portfolio

questions.explanation: Wx and Wy are the weights, that is the share of the portfolio invested in security X and security Y, and together they must total 100 percent. Option B is wrong because the expected returns are Rx and Ry, and Options A and C are risk measures that do not appear in the portfolio return formula.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A portfolio's expected return is:

options.a: The highest return among the securities in it
options.b: The sum of the returns of the securities in it
options.c: The simple average of the returns of the securities in it
options.d: The weighted average of the returns of the securities in it, weighted by the proportion of each security

questions.explanation: Portfolio return is a weighted average: each security's return is multiplied by the proportion of the portfolio invested in it, and the results are added. Option C would only be correct if every weight were equal, and Option B ignores the weights altogether.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: In portfolio theory, portfolio risk refers to:

options.a: The proportion of the portfolio held in the riskiest security only
options.b: The total amount of money invested in the portfolio
options.c: The relationships between the securities that make up the portfolio
options.d: The rate of return on treasury bills

questions.explanation: Portfolio risk depends on how the securities in the portfolio relate to one another, which is why combining securities can reduce risk. Option B is the size of the investment, not its risk, and Option D is the risk-free rate.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: An analyst builds a portfolio and writes the weights as 45% in security A and 45% in security B. What is wrong with this set of weights?

options.a: Weights must be stated in naira, never as percentages
options.b: Nothing is wrong, because equal weights are always required
options.c: The weights must total 100 percent, so 10% of the portfolio is unaccounted for
options.d: The weights must total 50 percent for a two-security portfolio

questions.explanation: The weights in a portfolio must add up to 100 percent because together they describe the whole amount invested; 45% plus 45% is only 90%. Option B is wrong because weights need not be equal, and Option A is wrong because naira amounts are converted into proportions before they are used.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The capital asset pricing model is built on the model of portfolio choice developed in 1959 by:
questions.explanation: CAPM grew out of Harry Markowitz's model of portfolio choice, which showed how investors can combine securities to balance return and risk. Option A is linked with market efficiency, while Options C and D are economists known for work on money and interest rather than portfolio choice.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The capital asset pricing model can be described as:
questions.explanation: CAPM is an equilibrium pricing model: it states the return a security should offer, given its systematic risk, when the market is in balance. Options B, C and D belong to other areas of financial management, namely bond valuation, project appraisal and the management of current assets respectively.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The main emphasis of the capital asset pricing model is on:

options.a: Calculating the working capital needed by a firm
options.b: Removing all risk from an investor's portfolio
options.c: Choosing the cheapest source of long-term finance
options.d: Pricing individual securities to determine the contribution each makes to the overall portfolio

questions.explanation: CAPM focuses on pricing individual securities, so that an investor can see what each security contributes to the whole portfolio. Option B is wrong because systematic risk can never be removed, and Options A and C belong to other topics.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes systematic risk from unsystematic risk?

options.a: Systematic risk can be diversified away, while unsystematic risk cannot
options.b: Neither is affected by the number of securities held
options.c: Both can be fully eliminated by holding enough securities
options.d: Systematic risk cannot be diversified away, while unsystematic risk can be reduced by diversification

questions.explanation: Systematic risk is uncontrollable and cannot be diversified away by any investor, while unsystematic risk is controllable and diversifiable. Option A reverses the two, and Option C is wrong because no amount of diversification removes systematic risk.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of systematic risk?

options.b: A strike by a company's employees

questions.explanation: A strike affects only the company concerned, so it is an unsystematic risk that diversification can reduce. Options A, C and D affect almost every security at once, which is what makes them systematic risks.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of unsystematic risk?

options.d: Raw material shortage at a firm

questions.explanation: War affects the whole economy and every investor, so it is a systematic risk that cannot be diversified away. Options A, C and D are problems inside particular companies, which makes them unsystematic.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Under CAPM, which of the following is classified as an unsystematic risk?
questions.explanation: Technological advancements are treated as unsystematic risk because they affect particular firms differently and can be diversified. Options B, C and D are all systematic risks that hit the whole market.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Shares of Ikorodu Paints Plc fall sharply after an internal fraud by its finance director is discovered. Shares of other listed companies are unaffected. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Company fraud is specific to one firm, so it is an unsystematic risk, and an investor holding many different shares would feel only a small part of the loss. Option B is wrong because the rest of the market was unaffected, and Options C and D are inputs to the CAPM equation, not types of risk.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A sudden rise in the general rate of inflation in Nigeria reduces the returns on almost all shares on the stock exchange. An investor holding 40 different shares still loses value. This is because:

options.a: The investor's portfolio had a beta of zero
options.b: The investor held too few shares to remove the risk
options.c: General inflation is a systematic risk that cannot be diversified away
options.d: General inflation is an unsystematic risk that the investor failed to diversify

questions.explanation: General inflation affects the whole market, so it is a systematic risk, and adding more shares does not remove it. Options B and D wrongly suggest more diversification would help, and Option A is wrong because a zero-beta portfolio would not move with the market at all.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Kano Agro Ltd and Enugu Textiles Plc each face separate problems: Kano Agro has a raw material shortage and Enugu Textiles has a sudden change of management. An investor wants to reduce exposure to risks like these. The best approach is to:

options.a: Hold only treasury bills and the shares of one of the firms
options.b: Wait for the general inflation rate to fall
options.c: Spread the investment across many different securities
options.d: Invest everything in whichever of the two firms has the higher beta

questions.explanation: A raw input shortage and a change of management are firm-specific, unsystematic risks, and these are controllable through diversification. Option D concentrates the risk instead of spreading it, and Option B confuses these firm problems with an economy-wide factor.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: In the CAPM equation E(Ri) = RF + (Rm - RF)Bi, the beta Bi represents:

options.a: The unsystematic risk of security i
options.b: The systematic risk of security i
options.c: The total amount invested in security i

questions.explanation: Beta measures the systematic risk of a security, that is how sensitive it is to movements in the whole market. Option A is wrong because CAPM does not reward unsystematic risk, which can be diversified, and Option D is RF.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: In the CAPM equation, the expression (Rm - RF) is called the:
questions.explanation: Rm minus RF is the extra return the market offers above the risk-free rate, known as the market risk premium. It is multiplied by beta and then added to RF. Option C is RF alone, and Option B is the whole equation, not this one term.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The equation E(Ri) = RF + (Rm - RF)Bi is also known as the:
questions.explanation: The CAPM equation is the security market line (SML), which shows the required return for each level of beta. Option A is a curve of efficient portfolios plotted against standard deviation, and Option B relates bond yields to maturity.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: When applying CAPM in Nigeria, the treasury bill rate is normally used as:

options.a: Bi, the beta of the security
options.b: Rm, the expected return of the market
options.d: E(Ri), the expected return of the security

questions.explanation: Treasury bills are short-term government securities with practically no default risk, so their rate is used as RF. Option B is the return on the stock market as a whole, which is a different input.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: In CAPM, Rm stands for:

options.a: The expected return of the market
options.d: The return on security m only

questions.explanation: Rm is the expected return on the market as a whole, such as the stock market return. Option C is RF, and Option B is Rm minus RF, not Rm alone.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: If a security's given (forecast) return is above the return on the security market line, the security is:
questions.explanation: A security offering more than the SML requires for its beta is a bargain, so it is underpriced and worth buying. Option B is the common trap: a return BELOW the SML means overpriced, not above.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: If a security's given return is below the return required by the security market line, the security is:
questions.explanation: A security that returns less than CAPM requires for its level of systematic risk is overpriced, so investors should avoid or sell it. Options A and B reverse the rule, since a bargain is one whose return is above the SML.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A security whose given return is exactly equal to its security market line return is said to be:
questions.explanation: When the given return equals the SML required return, the security offers exactly what its beta deserves, so it is correctly priced. Option D is wrong because a security on the SML can still carry systematic risk.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: An analyst finds that a share is underpriced according to CAPM. The appropriate advice to an investor is to:

options.a: Sell the share, because it offers less return than its risk requires
options.b: Buy the share, because it offers more return than its risk requires
options.c: Sell the share, because its beta must be negative
options.d: Ignore the share, because underpriced shares are always risk-free

questions.explanation: An underpriced share has a given return above its SML return, which makes it a bargain, so the advice is to buy. Option A describes an overpriced share, and Options C and D make claims about risk that pricing alone does not tell us.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: When computing a required return with CAPM, the correct order of working is to:

options.a: Divide Rm minus RF by beta, then add RF
options.b: Multiply Rm by beta first, then subtract RF
options.c: Find Rm minus RF first, multiply by beta, then add RF
options.d: Add RF to Rm first, then multiply by beta

questions.explanation: The market risk premium (Rm - RF) is found first, multiplied by beta, and then added to RF to give E(Ri). Option B applies beta to the whole market return, and Option A divides by beta, both of which give wrong required returns.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the assumptions of the capital asset pricing model?

options.a: Investors can borrow and lend freely at the risk-free rate
options.b: Investors pay taxes and transaction costs on every trade
options.d: All investors share the same single-period planning horizon

questions.explanation: CAPM assumes perfect markets with no taxes and no transaction costs, so a world with taxes and dealing costs on every trade contradicts the model. Options A, C and D are all standard CAPM assumptions.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Under the assumptions of CAPM, investors assess securities on the basis of:

options.a: Market price and number of shares

questions.explanation: CAPM assumes risk-averse investors who judge securities by their expected return and their risk measured by standard deviation. Options A, B and D are ratio and market measures that the model does not use as its basis of choice.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Which of the following is an assumption of the capital asset pricing model?

options.a: Investors cannot borrow at the risk-free rate
options.b: Securities can only be bought in large, indivisible blocks
options.c: All investors share the same forecasts of returns and risk
options.d: Different investors have different forecasts and planning horizons

questions.explanation: CAPM assumes all investors share the same single-period horizon and the same forecasts, called homogeneous expectations. Option B contradicts the assumption that securities are perfectly divisible, and Option A contradicts free borrowing and lending at the risk-free rate.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The CAPM assumption that 'securities are perfectly divisible' means that:

options.a: An investor can buy any fraction of a security, however small
options.b: Every security pays a dividend that can be divided among shareholders
options.c: Securities can be split into systematic and unsystematic parts
options.d: Each investor must hold an equal number of shares in every company

questions.explanation: Perfect divisibility means investments can be bought in any amount, so investors can hold exactly the portfolio weights they want. Option C confuses divisibility with the split of risk into its two types.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: In the CAPM equation, which input is specific to the individual security rather than common to all securities in the market?
questions.explanation: RF, Rm and therefore Rm - RF are the same for every security in a market, so the only security-specific input is beta. That is why two securities in the same market have different required returns only because their betas differ; Options A, C and D are shared inputs.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Which type of risk is rewarded with extra expected return under CAPM?

options.b: Unsystematic risk, measured by standard deviation

questions.explanation: CAPM adds a premium of (Rm - RF) x beta, so only systematic risk, measured by beta, earns extra return. Unsystematic risk can be diversified away at no cost, so Options B and C are wrong, and Option A ignores the premium altogether.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A security with a beta of 1.0 is expected to:

options.a: Move in the opposite direction to the market
options.b: Be twice as volatile as the market
options.c: Have no systematic risk at all
options.d: Move in line with the market, with the same systematic risk as the market

questions.explanation: The market itself has a beta of 1.0, so a security with beta 1.0 has the same systematic risk as the market and, under CAPM, a required return equal to Rm. Option C describes a beta of zero, and Option A describes a negative beta.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Share P has a beta of 1.6 and share Q has a beta of 0.7. Which statement is correct?

options.a: Q has more systematic risk than the market and P has less
options.b: P will always earn a lower return than Q
options.c: Both have less systematic risk than the market
options.d: P has more systematic risk than the market and Q has less

questions.explanation: A beta above 1 means a share is more sensitive to market movements than the market itself, and a beta below 1 means less sensitive. Option A reverses this, and Option B is wrong because, under CAPM, the higher-beta share P has the higher required return.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: As more securities with less than perfectly positive correlation are added to a portfolio, the portfolio's total risk:

options.a: Falls, until mainly systematic risk remains
options.b: Rises steadily with each security added
options.c: Falls to zero once about 20 securities are held
options.d: Stays the same, because risk depends only on beta

questions.explanation: Diversification removes unsystematic risk, so total risk falls as securities are added, but it levels off at the systematic risk that cannot be diversified away. Option C is wrong because systematic risk never disappears, and Option B is the opposite of the diversification effect.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Two-security portfolios are formed from shares with the same standard deviations but different correlation coefficients. Which correlation gives the GREATEST reduction in portfolio risk?
questions.explanation: The lower the correlation between two securities, the more their movements offset each other, and a correlation of -1.0 gives the greatest risk reduction (risk can even be eliminated with the right weights). Option A, perfect positive correlation, gives no risk reduction at all, and Options B and D give partial reduction.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: In portfolio theory, the efficient frontier is:

options.a: The set of portfolios that contain only risk-free assets
options.b: The set of portfolios with a beta of exactly 1.0
options.c: The line showing required return against beta for single securities
options.d: The set of portfolios that give the highest expected return for each level of risk

questions.explanation: The efficient frontier, from Markowitz's portfolio choice model, traces the portfolios that offer the most return for each level of risk (or the least risk for each return); no rational investor would choose a portfolio below it. Option C describes the security market line, which uses beta rather than total risk.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the capital market line (CML) from the security market line (SML)?

options.a: Both lines measure risk by the coefficient of variation
options.b: The CML plots return against beta; the SML plots return against standard deviation
options.c: The CML applies only to single securities; the SML applies only to portfolios
options.d: The CML plots return against standard deviation for efficient portfolios; the SML plots required return against beta for any security

questions.explanation: The CML measures risk by total risk (standard deviation) and applies to efficient portfolios that combine the market portfolio with the risk-free asset, while the SML measures risk by beta and prices any security. Option B swaps the two risk measures, and Option C reverses where each line applies.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised limitation of the capital asset pricing model?

options.a: Beta is usually estimated from past data and may not hold in future
options.b: It shows that unsystematic risk earns a higher return than systematic risk
options.c: Its assumptions of no taxes and no transaction costs are unrealistic
options.d: It is hard to identify a truly risk-free rate and the true market return

questions.explanation: CAPM says the opposite: only systematic risk earns a premium, so Option B is not a limitation but a misstatement of the model. Options A, C and D are genuine criticisms, since the perfect-market assumptions are unrealistic and the inputs RF, Rm and beta must be estimated.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The risk-free rate is 10%, the expected return on the market is 16% and a share has a beta of 1.5. Using CAPM, the share's required return is:
questions.explanation: E(R) = RF + (Rm - RF) x beta = 10% + (16% - 10%) x 1.5 = 10% + 9% = 19%. Option C multiplies the whole market return by beta instead of the market risk premium, and Option A forgets to add the risk-free rate.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Treasury bills yield 8% and the stock market is expected to return 14%. What is the required return on a share with a beta of 0.6?
questions.explanation: E(R) = 8% + (14% - 8%) x 0.6 = 8% + 3.6% = 11.6%. Option D divides the market risk premium by beta instead of multiplying, and Option C applies beta to the full 14% market return.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The risk-free rate is 9% and the expected market return is 15%. What is the CAPM required return on a share with a beta of 1.0?
questions.explanation: E(R) = 9% + (15% - 9%) x 1.0 = 15%, so a share with beta 1.0 requires exactly the market return. Option B is only the market risk premium, and Option A is the return for a beta of zero.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The risk-free rate is 11% and the expected market return is 17%. What is the CAPM required return on an investment with a beta of zero?
questions.explanation: With beta = 0, E(R) = 11% + (17% - 11%) x 0 = 11%, so an investment with no systematic risk earns only the risk-free rate. Option A forgets that RF is still added, and Option D is the return for a beta of 1.0.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Given RF = 0.07, Rm = 0.13 and a beta of 2.2, the expected return on the security using CAPM is (to 1 decimal place):
questions.explanation: E(R) = 0.07 + (0.13 - 0.07) x 2.2 = 0.07 + 0.132 = 0.202, or 20.2%. Option D multiplies 0.13 by beta instead of the premium 0.06, and Option B adds the premium to Rm instead of RF.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Lekki Logistics Plc has a beta of 1.2. The treasury bill rate is 12.5% and the stock market is expected to return 20%. The return shareholders require on Lekki Logistics shares is:
questions.explanation: E(R) = 12.5% + (20% - 12.5%) x 1.2 = 12.5% + 9% = 21.5%. Option A simply multiplies the market return by beta and ignores the risk-free rate, and Option D divides the premium by beta.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: An investor expects the market to return 11%, while government treasury bills pay 6%. A share has a beta of 1.8. By how many percentage points does the share's CAPM required return exceed the market's expected return?
questions.explanation: Required return = 6% + (11% - 6%) x 1.8 = 15%, which is 15% - 11% = 4 percentage points above the market. Option D is just the market risk premium, and Option A is the share's risk premium over RF, not over the market.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The expected return on the market is 18% and the risk-free rate is 11%. The market risk premium is:
questions.explanation: Market risk premium = Rm - RF = 18% - 11% = 7%, the extra return the market pays above the risk-free rate. Option A adds the two rates, and Option D is the market return itself, not the premium.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A share with a beta of 1.6 has a CAPM required return of 17%. If the risk-free rate is 9%, the market risk premium is:
questions.explanation: From E(R) = RF + (Rm - RF) x beta, (Rm - RF) = (E(R) - RF) / beta = (17% - 9%) / 1.6 = 5%. Option D is the share's own risk premium before dividing by beta, and Option B multiplies by beta instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A share has a CAPM required return of 20%. The risk-free rate is 8% and the expected market return is 16%. The share's beta is (to 2 decimal places):
questions.explanation: Rearranging CAPM, beta = (E(R) - RF) / (Rm - RF) = (20 - 8) / (16 - 8) = 12 / 8 = 1.5. Option A turns the fraction upside down, and Option B divides the share's return by the market return without removing RF.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A share has a CAPM required return of 13%. The risk-free rate is 10% and the expected market return is 16%. The share's beta is (to 2 decimal places):
questions.explanation: Rearranging CAPM, beta = (E(R) - RF) / (Rm - RF) = (13 - 10) / (16 - 10) = 3 / 6 = 0.5. Option D turns the fraction upside down, and Option C divides the share's return by the market return without removing RF.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A share has a CAPM required return of 15.6%. The risk-free rate is 12% and the expected market return is 18%. The share's beta is (to 2 decimal places):
questions.explanation: Rearranging CAPM, beta = (E(R) - RF) / (Rm - RF) = (15.6 - 12) / (18 - 12) = 3.6 / 6 = 0.6. Option B turns the fraction upside down, and Option D divides the share's return by the market return without removing RF.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A share with a beta of 0.5 has a CAPM required return of 14% when the expected market return is 18%. The risk-free rate is:
questions.explanation: E(R) = RF + (Rm - RF) x beta gives 14 = RF + (18 - RF) x 0.5 = 0.5RF + 9, so 0.5RF = 5 and RF = 10%. Option A stops at 5% and forgets that RF also appears inside the bracket, and Option B is just the gap between the two returns.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The market risk premium is 6%. A share with a beta of 1.4 has a CAPM required return of 18.4%. The risk-free rate is:
questions.explanation: RF = E(R) - (Rm - RF) x beta = 18.4% - 6% x 1.4 = 18.4% - 8.4% = 10%. Option D subtracts the premium without multiplying by beta, and Option A is the share's risk premium, not the risk-free rate.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A share with a beta of 1.5 has a CAPM required return of 22%. The risk-free rate is 10%. The expected return on the market is:
questions.explanation: (Rm - RF) = (E(R) - RF) / beta = (22 - 10) / 1.5 = 8%, so Rm = 10% + 8% = 18%. Option A is only the market risk premium, and Option B multiplies by beta instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A defensive share with a beta of 0.85 has a CAPM required return of 12.4% when the risk-free rate is 9%. The expected market return is (to 2 decimal places):
questions.explanation: (Rm - RF) = (12.4 - 9) / 0.85 = 4%, so Rm = 9% + 4% = 13%. Option A multiplies the share's premium by beta, and Option D gives only the market risk premium.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: RF = 10%, Rm = 15%. Share J has a beta of 1.2 and an analyst forecasts its return at 17%. According to CAPM, share J is:

options.a: Overpriced, because its SML return is 28%
options.b: Correctly priced, because its SML return is 17%
options.c: Underpriced, because its SML return is 16%
options.d: Overpriced, because its SML return is 16%

questions.explanation: SML return = 10% + (15% - 10%) x 1.2 = 16%. The forecast 17% is above 16%, so J offers more than its risk requires and is underpriced. Option D gets the number right but reverses the rule, and Option A multiplies the full market return by beta.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The treasury bill rate is 9% and the market return is 14%. Security K has a beta of 1.8 and a given return of 17%. Security K is:

options.a: Overpriced, because its given return is below its SML return of 18%
options.b: Correctly priced, because its SML return is 17%
options.c: Underpriced, because its given return is above its SML return of 11.78%
options.d: Underpriced, because its given return is above the market return of 14%

questions.explanation: SML return = 9% + (14% - 9%) x 1.8 = 18%. The given 17% is below 18%, so K is overpriced. Option D wrongly compares the return with Rm instead of the SML for K's own beta, and Option C divides the premium by beta.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: RF = 12% and Rm = 17%. Security L has a beta of 0.6 and its expected return is estimated at 15%. Security L is:

options.a: Risk-free, because its beta is below 1

questions.explanation: SML return = 12% + (17% - 12%) x 0.6 = 12% + 3% = 15%, exactly equal to the estimated 15%, so L is correctly priced. Option B might come from comparing 15% with Rm of 17%, and Option A is wrong because any positive beta carries systematic risk.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The risk-free rate is 8% and the market return is 13%. Three shares have the following betas and forecast returns: A (beta 0.8, 13%), B (beta 1.4, 14%), C (beta 2.0, 18%). Which share(s) are underpriced?
questions.explanation: SML returns are A: 8% + 5% x 0.8 = 12%, B: 8% + 5% x 1.4 = 15% and C: 8% + 5% x 2.0 = 18%. Only A's forecast (13%) is above its SML return, so only A is underpriced; B is below its SML (overpriced) and C is exactly on it (correctly priced), which rules out Options B and C.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: RF = 11% and Rm = 16%. Securities X, Y and Z have betas of 0.4, 1.0 and 1.6 and given returns of 14%, 16% and 18% respectively. Which security is overpriced?
questions.explanation: SML returns: X = 11% + 5% x 0.4 = 13%, Y = 11% + 5% x 1.0 = 16%, Z = 11% + 5% x 1.6 = 19%. Z's given 18% is below its 19% SML return, so Z is overpriced. X is above its SML (underpriced) and Y is on it (correctly priced), so Options C and D are wrong.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: RF = 10%, Rm = 16%. A share with a beta of 0.9 is forecast to return 17.5%. By how much is the forecast return above or below the share's SML return?
questions.explanation: SML return = 10% + (16% - 10%) x 0.9 = 15.4%, so the forecast 17.5% is 17.5 - 15.4 = 2.1 percentage points above the SML (the share is underpriced). Option A compares with Rm instead, and Option C comes from multiplying the whole market return by beta.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Treasury bills yield 7% and the market is expected to return 12%. Ota Breweries Plc has a beta of 1.5, and its shares are expected to return 13%. Which option correctly gives the required return and the pricing verdict?
questions.explanation: Required return = 7% + (12% - 7%) x 1.5 = 14.5%. The expected 13% is below 14.5%, so the share is overpriced. Option B has the right figure but the wrong verdict, Option A multiplies Rm by beta, and Option C forgets to add RF.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A share's possible returns are 10% (probability 0.3), 18% (probability 0.5) and 26% (probability 0.2). Its beta is 1.5, RF = 9% and Rm = 15%. Comparing its expected return with its CAPM required return, the share is:

options.a: Overpriced, since its expected return of 17.2% is below the required 18%
options.b: Underpriced, since its expected return of 17.2% is above the market return of 15%
options.c: Correctly priced, since its expected return of 18% equals the required return
options.d: Underpriced, since its expected return of 17.2% is above the required 13%

questions.explanation: Expected return = 0.3 x 10% + 0.5 x 18% + 0.2 x 26% = 17.2%, and required return = 9% + (15% - 9%) x 1.5 = 18%. Since 17.2% is below 18%, the share is overpriced. Option B compares with Rm instead of the SML return for this beta, and Option C uses a simple average of the returns.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A portfolio is made up of 60% in security X, expected to return 15%, and 40% in security Y, expected to return 25%. The expected return on the portfolio is:
questions.explanation: PR = WxRx + WyRy = (0.6 x 15%) + (0.4 x 25%) = 9% + 10% = 19%. Option A is a simple average that ignores the weights, Option C attaches the weights to the wrong securities, and Option B adds the returns.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Security A is expected to return 12% and security B 20%. If an investor puts 25% of his funds in A and 75% in B, the portfolio's expected return is:
questions.explanation: PR = (0.25 x 12%) + (0.75 x 20%) = 3% + 15% = 18%. Option A reverses the weights, and Option C is the simple average of the two returns.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Mrs Adebayo invests N300,000 in Ilorin Cement shares, expected to return 14%, and N700,000 in Benin Foods shares, expected to return 24%. The expected return on her portfolio is:
questions.explanation: The weights are 300,000/1,000,000 = 0.3 and 700,000/1,000,000 = 0.7, so PR = (0.3 x 14%) + (0.7 x 24%) = 4.2% + 16.8% = 21%. Option D ignores the different amounts invested, and Option C attaches the larger weight to the lower-return share.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: An investor holds N450,000 in share L, expected to return 10%, and N150,000 in share M, expected to return 22%. The expected return on the portfolio is:
questions.explanation: Total invested is N600,000, so the weights are 450/600 = 0.75 and 150/600 = 0.25. PR = (0.75 x 10%) + (0.25 x 22%) = 7.5% + 5.5% = 13%. Option B is the unweighted average, and Option A swaps the weights.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A portfolio contains three securities: 50% in P (expected return 12%), 30% in Q (18%) and 20% in R (25%). The portfolio's expected return is:
questions.explanation: E(Rp) = SUM[wi x E(Ri)] = (0.5 x 12%) + (0.3 x 18%) + (0.2 x 25%) = 6% + 5.4% + 5% = 16.4%. Option D is the simple average of the three returns, and Option A attaches 50% to R and 20% to P.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: An investment club invests N200,000 in share A (expected return 10%), N300,000 in share B (16%) and N500,000 in share C (22%). The expected return on the club's portfolio is:
questions.explanation: Total is N1,000,000, giving weights of 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5. E(Rp) = (0.2 x 10%) + (0.3 x 16%) + (0.5 x 22%) = 2% + 4.8% + 11% = 17.8%. Option A is the simple average, and Option C attaches the largest weight to the lowest-return share.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: An investor places N2,000,000 in a portfolio, 40% in share S (expected return 15%) and 60% in share T (expected return 20%). The expected return on the portfolio in naira is:
questions.explanation: Portfolio return = (0.4 x 15%) + (0.6 x 20%) = 6% + 12% = 18%, and 18% of N2,000,000 = N360,000. Option D uses the simple average of 17.5%, and Option B swaps the weights to get 17%.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Security X is expected to return 10% and security Y 22%. What proportion of a two-security portfolio must be invested in Y to achieve an expected return of 17% (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.explanation: Let w be the weight in Y: 10(1 - w) + 22w = 17, so 12w = 7 and w = 7/12 = 58.33%. Option B is the weight in X, and Option D divides the target by Y's return, ignoring X altogether.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Share A is expected to return 8% and share B 20%. To earn 17% on a portfolio of only A and B, the proportion invested in A must be:
questions.explanation: With weight w in B, 8(1 - w) + 20w = 17, so 12w = 9 and w = 75% in B, leaving 25% in A. Option B is the weight in B, not A, and Option A divides the target return by B's return.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: RF = 10% and Rm = 15%. Share L has a beta of 0.6 and share M a beta of 1.8. Using their SML returns, what is the expected return on a portfolio of 40% L and 60% M?
questions.explanation: SML returns are L = 10% + 5% x 0.6 = 13% and M = 10% + 5% x 1.8 = 19%. PR = (0.4 x 13%) + (0.6 x 19%) = 5.2% + 11.4% = 16.6%. Option C swaps the weights, and Option D comes from multiplying the full market return by beta when finding each SML return.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The treasury bill rate is 9% and the market return is 13%. An investor puts 70% of her funds in share G (beta 0.5) and 30% in share H (beta 2.0). Using CAPM returns, the expected portfolio return is:
questions.explanation: CAPM returns are G = 9% + 4% x 0.5 = 11% and H = 9% + 4% x 2.0 = 17%. PR = (0.7 x 11%) + (0.3 x 17%) = 12.8%. Option D ignores the weights, and Option B attaches 70% to H instead of G.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A portfolio is invested 40% in a share with a beta of 0.9 and 60% in a share with a beta of 1.4. The portfolio beta is:
questions.explanation: A portfolio's beta is the weighted average of the individual betas: (0.4 x 0.9) + (0.6 x 1.4) = 0.36 + 0.84 = 1.2. Option C is the simple average, and Option B attaches the weights to the wrong shares.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A pension fund holds N500,000 in share A (beta 1.2), N300,000 in share B (beta 0.8) and N200,000 in share C (beta 1.5). The beta of the fund's portfolio is:
questions.explanation: Weights are 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 of the N1,000,000 total, so portfolio beta = (0.5 x 1.2) + (0.3 x 0.8) + (0.2 x 1.5) = 0.6 + 0.24 + 0.3 = 1.14. Option C is the simple average of the betas, and Option A attaches 50% to C instead of A.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A portfolio is split equally between a share with a beta of 0.8 and a share with a beta of 1.6. If RF = 10% and Rm = 15%, the CAPM required return on the portfolio is:
questions.explanation: Portfolio beta = (0.5 x 0.8) + (0.5 x 1.6) = 1.2, so E(Rp) = 10% + (15% - 10%) x 1.2 = 16%. Option C assumes a beta of 1.0, Option D multiplies the full market return by beta, and Option B leaves out RF.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: An investor holds a fund with a beta of 1 and wants to combine it with a share of beta 1.8 so that the overall portfolio beta is 1.32. What proportion of the portfolio must be in the beta 1.8 share?
questions.explanation: With weight w in the share, (1 - w) x 1.0 + w x 1.8 = 1.32, so 0.8w = 0.32 and w = 40%. Option A is the weight left in the fund, and Option C divides the target beta by 1.8 without allowing for the fund's own beta.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The covariance between the returns on share Z and the market is 0.0048. The variance of market returns is 0.004 and the variance of share Z's returns is 0.009. Taking beta as covariance(Z, market) / variance(market), the beta of share Z is:
questions.explanation: Beta = Cov(Z, M) / Var(M) = 0.0048 / 0.004 = 1.2. Option D turns the fraction upside down, Option C divides by the share's own variance, and Option A is the correlation coefficient, which divides by both standard deviations.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Share W has a standard deviation of 24%, the market has a standard deviation of 16%, and the correlation between them is 0.5. Taking beta = correlation x (SD of share / SD of market), the beta of W is:
questions.explanation: Beta = 0.5 x (24 / 16) = 0.5 x 1.5 = 0.75. Option C leaves out the correlation, and Option D puts the market's standard deviation on top instead of the share's.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A portfolio is 60% in share A (standard deviation 20%) and 40% in share B (standard deviation 30%). The correlation between A and B is 0.2. Using Var(p) = wA^2 SDA^2 + wB^2 SDB^2 + 2 wA wB r SDA SDB, the portfolio standard deviation is (to 2 decimal places):
questions.explanation: Var(p) = (0.36 x 400) + (0.16 x 900) + (2 x 0.6 x 0.4 x 0.2 x 20 x 30) = 144 + 144 + 57.6 = 345.6, so SD = square root of 345.6 = 18.59%. Option A is the weighted average of the standard deviations, which is only correct when the correlation is +1, and Option D leaves out the covariance term.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Shares A and B have standard deviations of 12% and 18% and are perfectly negatively correlated (correlation -1). What proportion of the portfolio must be in A to make the portfolio's risk zero?
questions.explanation: With correlation -1, portfolio SD = |wA x 12 - wB x 18|, which is zero when wA x 12 = (1 - wA) x 18, giving wA = 18 / (12 + 18) = 60%. Option B is the weight in B, and Option D would leave the riskier share B dominating, so risk would not be zero.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: A portfolio is split 50:50 between two shares with standard deviations of 10% and 20%. If the returns on the two shares are perfectly positively correlated (correlation +1), the portfolio standard deviation is:
questions.explanation: With correlation +1 there is no diversification benefit, so the portfolio SD is simply the weighted average: (0.5 x 10%) + (0.5 x 20%) = 15%. Option C is the result for zero correlation and Option A is the result for correlation -1, both of which show risk falling only when correlation is below +1.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Using the capital market line E(Rp) = RF + [(Rm - RF) / SDm] x SDp, with RF = 10%, Rm = 18%, market standard deviation 20% and an efficient portfolio standard deviation of 15%, the expected portfolio return is:
questions.explanation: E(Rp) = 10% + (8% / 20%) x 15% = 10% + 0.4 x 15% = 16%. Option C turns the risk ratio upside down, and Option B forgets to add the risk-free rate.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: RF = 11% and Rm = 17%. Share D has a beta of 1.5 and share E a beta of 0.5. The difference between their CAPM required returns is:
questions.explanation: D requires 11% + 6% x 1.5 = 20% and E requires 11% + 6% x 0.5 = 14%, a difference of 6 percentage points, which equals the 6% premium times the beta gap of 1.0. Option B is only the beta gap, and Option C applies the betas to the full market return.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: If the market risk premium rises because Rm increases from 19% to 21% while RF stays at 13%, what is the new required return on a share with a beta of 1.25?
questions.explanation: The new premium is 21% - 13% = 8%, so E(R) = 13% + 8% x 1.25 = 13% + 10% = 23%. Option B is the old required return using a 6% premium, and Option D leaves beta out of the calculation.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: RF = 10% and Rm = 16%. If a share's beta doubles from 0.75 to 1.5, its CAPM required return:

options.b: Stays at 14.5%, because RF and Rm are unchanged

questions.explanation: Old return = 10% + 6% x 0.75 = 14.5%; new return = 10% + 6% x 1.5 = 19%. Only the risk premium part doubles (from 4.5% to 9%), so Option A is wrong to double the whole return, and Option C multiplies the full market return by beta.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Using CAPM with RF = 10% and Rm = 14%, what is the required return on a share whose beta is 0.5?
questions.explanation: E(R) = 10% + (14% - 10%) x 0.5 = 10% + 2% = 12%. A beta below 1 gives a required return between RF and Rm. Option A multiplies the market return by beta, and Option C divides the premium by beta.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: The treasury bill rate is 14% and the stock market return is 22%. Three shares have betas and forecast returns as follows: Ade (0.5, 19%), Bisi (1.5, 26%), Chidi (2.5, 33%). Which of them is correctly priced?
questions.explanation: SML returns: Ade = 14% + 8% x 0.5 = 18%, Bisi = 14% + 8% x 1.5 = 26%, Chidi = 14% + 8% x 2.5 = 34%. Only Bisi's forecast equals its SML return; Ade is above (underpriced) and Chidi is below (overpriced), so Options A and D are wrong.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: RF = 10% and Rm = 18%. Shares P, Q and R have betas of 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 and forecast returns of 16%, 19% and 21%. Which share offers the largest return above its SML return?
questions.explanation: SML returns are P = 10% + 8% x 0.5 = 14%, Q = 10% + 8% x 1.0 = 18% and R = 10% + 8% x 1.5 = 22%. The gaps are P +2, Q +1 and R -1 percentage points, so P is the most underpriced. Option D might be chosen because R has the highest forecast return, but R is actually below its SML and so overpriced.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model and Portfolio Theory
questions.question: Two correctly priced shares lie on the security market line. Share M has a beta of 0.8 and a return of 14.8%, and share N has a beta of 1.6 and a return of 19.6%. The market risk premium is:
questions.explanation: Along the SML each extra unit of beta adds one market risk premium, so (Rm - RF) = (19.6 - 14.8) / (1.6 - 0.8) = 4.8 / 0.8 = 6% (and RF = 14.8 - 6 x 0.8 = 10%). Option C is the gap in returns without dividing by the gap in beta, Option D wrongly divides a whole return by beta, while Option B divides by N's beta instead of the beta gap.

questions.question: The cost of capital refers to:

options.a: The cost of operating a business

questions.explanation: The cost of capital is the return a firm must pay to obtain funds, such as interest on debt or the return shareholders expect. Option A is general operating cost, and C is the cost of the goods a firm sells.

questions.question: Capital budgeting is primarily concerned with:
questions.explanation: Capital budgeting is the process of evaluating and choosing long-term investments, such as new machinery or a new factory, that will bring returns over many years. Managing daily expenses (A) is working capital management, and C and D belong to marketing and human resources.

questions.question: Which of the following is a capital budgeting technique?
questions.explanation: Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is used to evaluate long-term investment projects, which makes it a capital budgeting technique. The debt-to-equity ratio (B) and current ratio (C) are financial ratios, and the cash conversion cycle (D) is a working capital measure, so none of them are used to appraise projects.

questions.question: A project has a cost of N53,500 and its expected net cash inflows are N11,500 per annum for 6 years. If the cost of capital is 5%, the project's Net Present Value (NPV) is
questions.explanation: NPV = PV of inflows - cost. PV of inflows = 11,500 x [1 - (1.05)^-6] / 0.05 = 11,500 x 5.0757 = N58,370.46, so NPV = 58,370.46 - 53,500 = N4,870.46. Option C (N58,370.46) is only the present value of the inflows before subtracting the cost, and A and B are wrong totals.

questions.question: A financial metric that assesses an investment's profitability by comparing the present value of its expected future cash flows with its initial investment cost is called the:
questions.explanation: Net present value discounts the future cash flows to today and deducts the initial investment cost, so it shows whether a project would be profitable. Payback (A) only counts how long it takes to recover the outlay, and ARR (C) uses accounting profit rather than discounted cash flows. A future value (B) compounds forward instead of discounting back.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how a project's net present value is obtained?

options.a: Add up the expected future cash flows and deduct the initial investment cost
options.b: Divide the average annual accounting profit by the initial investment and multiply by 100
options.c: Compound the initial investment forward and compare it with the total future cash flows
options.d: Discount the expected future cash flows to present value and deduct the initial investment cost

questions.explanation: NPV converts each future cash flow into present value using the cost of capital and then subtracts the initial outlay. Option A ignores the time value of money because the cash flows are not discounted, and option B is the accounting rate of return. Option C works in future values and is not how NPV is defined.

questions.question: In the formula NPV = SUM[At / (1 + r)^n] - C0, what does C0 represent?

options.a: The initial outlay or investment cost
options.b: The cash flow at time t
options.c: The number of years of the project
options.d: The rate or cost of capital

questions.explanation: C0 is the cost paid at the start (time 0), which is why it is deducted after the future cash flows have been discounted. At (B) is the cash flow received at time t, r (D) is the cost of capital used for discounting, and n (C) is the number of years.

questions.question: In NPV analysis, the rate r used to discount a project's future cash flows is normally the:

options.c: Project's payback period expressed as a percentage

questions.explanation: The cash flows are discounted at the cost of capital, the return the firm's providers of finance require, so a positive NPV means the project earns more than that cost. The ARR (A) is an output of a different appraisal method, not the discount rate. Inflation alone (D) and the payback period (C) do not measure the required return on the firm's funds.

questions.question: Which expression gives the present value (discount) factor for a cash flow received at the end of year n when the cost of capital is r?
questions.explanation: The discount factor 1 / (1 + r)^n turns a single future amount into today's value under compound interest. Option A is the compound (future value) factor, the reverse of discounting. Option C is the present value annuity factor for a constant stream, and option D uses simple interest, which is not how cash flows are discounted in NPV.

questions.question: A project's annual cash inflow is the same amount every year for five years. The quickest correct way to find the present value of these inflows is to:

options.a: Multiply the annual cash inflow by the number of years
options.b: Multiply the annual cash inflow by the discount factor for year 5 only
options.c: Multiply the annual cash inflow by the present value annuity factor [1 - (1 + r)^-n] / r
options.d: Divide the annual cash inflow by the cost of capital

questions.explanation: When the cash flow is constant, the annuity factor adds up all the yearly discount factors in one step, so PV = annual inflow x [1 - (1 + r)^-n] / r. Option A ignores discounting altogether, and option B treats all five payments as if they arrived in year 5. Option D is the perpetuity formula, which assumes the inflow continues forever.

questions.question: Under the NPV decision rule, a project whose NPV is positive should be:

options.b: Postponed until its NPV becomes zero
options.c: Accepted only if its payback period is under two years

questions.explanation: A positive NPV means the discounted inflows exceed the initial outlay, so the project adds value and should be accepted. Rejecting it (D) is the rule for a negative NPV. The NPV rule does not add a payback condition (C), and there is no reason to wait for the NPV to fall to zero (B).

questions.question: Ijebu Plastics Ltd appraises a new moulding machine at its 14% cost of capital and finds an NPV of -N2.3 million. Based on the NPV rule, the company should:

options.a: Accept the machine, because a negative NPV means the outlay is recovered quickly
options.b: Reject the machine, because the present value of its inflows is less than its cost
options.c: Accept the machine, because any project with cash inflows should be undertaken
options.d: Accept the machine, provided its IRR is above zero

questions.explanation: A negative NPV shows that the discounted inflows fall short of the initial outlay, so the project would reduce the firm's value and is rejected. Options A and C accept a project the NPV rule rejects, and option A also misreads what a negative NPV means. Option D is wrong because an IRR above zero but below 14% still leaves a negative NPV.

questions.question: A project has an NPV of exactly zero at the firm's cost of capital. Which statement about it is correct under the NPV rules?

options.a: Its payback period is exactly equal to its life
options.b: It earns exactly the cost of capital, and it may still be worth undertaking, for example to build experience or a portfolio
options.c: It earns a return above the cost of capital and must be ranked first
options.d: It must be rejected because it makes a loss equal to its initial outlay

questions.explanation: At a zero NPV the discounted inflows exactly cover the outlay, so the project earns exactly the cost of capital; it is worth undertaking to build experience or a portfolio. Option D is wrong because a zero NPV is not a loss of the outlay. Option C describes a positive NPV, and option A confuses NPV with payback.

questions.question: Projects that cannot be undertaken together, so that accepting one means rejecting the other, are called:
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive projects compete for the same purpose, such as two alternative sites for one factory, so only one can be chosen. Independent projects (C) can each be accepted on their own merits. Contingent projects (A) depend on another project going ahead, and 'annuity projects' (D) simply describes even cash flows.

questions.question: Lekki Cold Stores must choose ONE of three alternative refrigeration systems. At its cost of capital the NPVs are: System P N4.2 million, System Q N6.8 million and System R N5.1 million. Which should it choose?

options.b: All three systems, since every NPV is positive

questions.explanation: Because only one system can be installed, the projects are mutually exclusive and the one with the highest NPV, System Q at N6.8 million, is chosen. Systems P (A) and R (C) add less value. Option B would be right only for independent projects with no budget limit.

questions.question: Kaduna Agro Ltd has no shortage of funds and is considering three INDEPENDENT projects with NPVs of N1.5 million, -N0.4 million and N0.2 million. Which decision is correct?

options.a: Reject all three, because one of them has a negative NPV
options.b: Accept only the project with the NPV of N1.5 million
options.c: Accept all three, because their total NPV is positive
options.d: Accept the projects with NPVs of N1.5 million and N0.2 million and reject the other

questions.explanation: Independent projects do not compete with each other, so each one with a positive NPV is accepted and each one with a negative NPV is rejected. Option B applies the mutually exclusive rule of choosing only the highest NPV. Options C and A wrongly judge the projects as a group instead of one by one.

questions.question: The discount rate at which a project's NPV is exactly zero is the project's:
questions.explanation: The IRR is the rate that makes the present value of the inflows equal the initial outlay, so NPV is zero at that rate; linear interpolation between a positive-NPV rate and a negative-NPV rate estimates it. The ARR (A) is based on accounting profit, and the profitability index (B) is a ratio, not a rate. The cost of capital (D) is the firm's required return, which the IRR is compared against.

questions.question: Using the internal rate of return method, an independent project should be accepted when:
