options.a: Regular contributions are professionally invested and later paid out as a pension
options.b: Contributions are kept as idle cash and returned without any growth
options.c: Members borrow from the pool at low interest during their working years
options.d: The government pays all retirees from taxes with no member contributions

questions.explanation: In a pension fund, employees and employers make regular contributions into a retirement savings account, which is invested to grow and is later distributed as a pension. Option C describes a cooperative loan scheme, and option B ignores the investment that makes the fund grow. Option D describes a pay-as-you-go state arrangement with no contributions, not a pension fund.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under Nigeria's Pension Reform Act 2014, what is the minimum total contribution (employer plus employee) to an employee's retirement savings account, as a percentage of monthly emoluments?
questions.explanation: The Pension Reform Act 2014 sets a minimum of 10% from the employer and 8% from the employee, a combined 18% of monthly emoluments. Option A (15%) was the combined rate under the earlier 2004 Act. Options C and B are only the employer's and the employee's shares on their own.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under Nigeria's Contributory Pension Scheme (Pension Reform Act 2014), the pension contributions of an employee must be privately managed by:

options.a: Any commercial bank the employee chooses

questions.explanation: Contributions under the scheme are managed exclusively by a licensed (registered) pension fund administrator, which opens the employee's retirement savings account and invests the money. Option D is wrong because the employer only deducts and remits the contributions, it does not manage them. Options A and C are not licensed to administer pension funds under the scheme.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of a pension fund administrator?

options.a: Paying retirement benefits to the retiree
options.b: Keeping safe custody of the pension assets on trust
options.c: Investing and managing pension fund assets
options.d: Opening a retirement savings account for the employee

questions.explanation: Safe custody of pension assets is the job of the pension fund custodian, which holds the assets and acts on the administrator's instructions. Opening the retirement savings account (D), investing and managing the assets (C) and paying retirement benefits (A) are all functions of the pension fund administrator.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which of the following is a function of a pension fund administrator?

options.a: Providing regular account statements and updates on fund transactions
options.c: Setting the minimum contribution rates for all employers
options.d: Deducting contributions from workers' salaries at source

questions.explanation: A pension fund administrator keeps contributors informed by sending regular statements and updates on transactions in their accounts. Options C and B belong to the law and the regulator (the National Pension Commission), not to an administrator. Option D is the employer's duty, since the employer deducts and remits the contributions.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Adaeze's employer remits her pension contributions every month. One firm invests the money and pays her benefits, while a separate firm holds the pension assets in safe keeping and settles trades only on the first firm's instructions. Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, the second firm is a:
questions.explanation: A pension fund custodian keeps pension assets in safe custody, separate from the administrator, and acts on the administrator's instructions. Option A, the administrator, is the first firm that invests and pays benefits. Options C and B are roles in collective investment schemes and share trading, not the holder of pension assets.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which body regulates and supervises pension fund administrators and custodians under Nigeria's Pension Reform Act 2014?
questions.explanation: The National Pension Commission (PenCom) superintends the Contributory Pension Scheme, licenses administrators and custodians and can intervene in their management. Option D regulates the capital market and collective investment schemes such as unit trusts, not pension operators. Options C and A are a stock exchange group and the company registry.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: The Pension Reform Act 2014, which now governs Nigeria's Contributory Pension Scheme, repealed which earlier law?

options.b: The Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020
options.d: The Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act 2020

questions.explanation: The Pension Reform Act 2014, signed on 1 July 2014, repealed the Pension Reform Act 2004 that first set up the scheme. Option A is a capital market law (itself later replaced in 2025), and options B and D govern companies and banks, not pensions.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A pension plan that promises a specific, guaranteed monthly payout on retirement, calculated from the worker's salary history and years of service, is a:
questions.explanation: A defined benefit plan fixes the pension itself in advance using a formula based on salary and years of service. Option B fixes only the contributions, so the payout varies with investment performance. Option A is a flexible plan for self-employed or informal workers, and option C is a type of mutual fund.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A pension plan with fixed contributions, in which the final retirement payout rises or falls with the performance of the funds invested, is a:
questions.explanation: In a defined contribution (contributory) plan, what is fixed is the amount paid in; the amount paid out depends on how well the invested money performs. Options B and D guarantee the payout instead, a final salary scheme being a form of defined benefit plan. Option C pays pensions from current income rather than from invested contributions.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: In which type of pension plan does the employee bear the investment risk, because a poor investment performance directly reduces the retirement payout?
questions.explanation: In a defined contribution plan the payout depends on how the invested contributions perform, so weak returns reduce the employee's pension and the risk sits with the employee. In a defined benefit plan (A), including a final salary scheme (D), the payout is promised, so the employer or sponsor must make up any shortfall. Option B also describes a promised payout.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: In a defined benefit pension plan, who bears the risk that the invested funds perform poorly?

options.a: The employee, whose pension falls when returns fall
options.b: No one, because defined benefit funds are not invested
options.c: The pension fund custodian, who must refund any losses
options.d: The employer or plan sponsor, who must still pay the promised benefit

questions.explanation: Because a defined benefit plan guarantees the payout, the sponsor (usually the employer) must fund the promised pension even if investments do badly. Option A describes a defined contribution plan. Option C is wrong because a custodian only holds assets safely, and option B is wrong because defined benefit funds are normally invested too.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Kunle is a self-employed tailor in Aba with irregular income. He wants to save for retirement in a flexible way. Which type of pension plan is designed for him?
questions.explanation: A personal or informal pension plan is designed for self-employed people and informal sector workers to save for retirement flexibly. Option B is normally offered by an employer and promises a salary-based payout, which Kunle does not have. Option D is life insurance cover, not retirement savings, and option C is a listed investment fund, not a pension plan.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: At retirement, Mrs Okafor learns that her pension depends entirely on the balance in her retirement savings account, which grew from her and her employer's fixed contributions and the returns earned on them. Her plan is best described as a:
questions.explanation: Fixed contributions plus whatever the investments earned, with no promised payout, is the mark of a defined contribution plan. Option A would have promised her a specific amount based on salary and years of service. Option B is wrong because her pension comes from an accumulated, invested balance, and option C is an investment pool, not a pension plan.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A pension plan in which benefits are paid out of an accumulated pool of contributions that has been set aside and invested in advance is described as:
questions.explanation: A funded plan builds up a pool of assets from contributions before benefits fall due, and pays pensions from that pool. Options B and C describe the opposite arrangement, where pensions are paid from the sponsor's current income or current contributions. Option D is wrong because a defined benefit plan can be either funded or unfunded.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A state government pays its retired workers' pensions each month directly out of that month's revenue, without any invested pool of assets. This pension arrangement is:
questions.explanation: When pensions are paid from current revenue rather than from assets set aside in advance, the plan is unfunded (pay-as-you-go). Option D requires an accumulated, invested pool. Option C is wrong because a contribution plan pays out of each member's own invested balance, and option B is a mutual fund type.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under Nigeria's Contributory Pension Scheme (Pension Reform Act 2014), each employee's contributions go into an individual retirement savings account that is invested and paid out at retirement. This scheme is therefore best described as:
questions.explanation: Contributions are fixed percentages of emoluments and accumulate in an invested individual account, so the scheme is funded, and the payout depends on the account balance, so it is defined contribution. Option A describes a pay-as-you-go guaranteed pension. Option B wrongly implies a guaranteed payout, and option C wrongly implies there is no invested pool.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, within what period after paying salaries must an employer deduct and remit employees' pension contributions?
questions.explanation: The Pension Reform Act 2014 requires employers to remit the deducted contributions within 7 working days of paying salaries, and late remittance attracts a penalty. Options D, B and A are not the deadline set by the Act.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, a private sector employer is required to join the Contributory Pension Scheme if it has at least how many employees?
questions.explanation: The 2014 Act raised the threshold for compulsory participation of private sector employers to 15 employees, from 5 under the earlier law. Option B is the old 2004 threshold, and options A and C are not the figure in the Act; employees of smaller firms may still join voluntarily.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, the monthly emoluments on which pension contributions are based must not be less than the total of:

options.b: Basic salary, housing allowance and transport allowance

questions.explanation: The Act treats monthly emoluments as the total emoluments in the contract of employment, but never less than basic pay plus housing and transport allowances. Option A leaves out the two allowances, and options D and C include items that are not part of this minimum base.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, an employee who resigns or is disengaged and remains without a job for 4 months may withdraw what share of the balance in his or her retirement savings account?
questions.explanation: The 2014 Act allows a person who retires voluntarily, resigns or is disengaged, and stays unemployed for 4 months, to access 25% of the retirement savings account balance. Options B, C and A are not the percentage in the Act; withdrawing everything would defeat the purpose of saving for retirement.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, the minimum contributions are 10% of monthly emoluments from the employer and 8% from the employee. Tola's monthly emoluments are N250,000. What is the minimum total amount that should be paid into her retirement savings account each month?
questions.explanation: Total contribution = (10% + 8%) x monthly emoluments = 0.18 x 250,000 = N45,000. Option A is only the employer's 10% and option C only the employee's 8%. Option D uses the old combined rate of 15%.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014 the employee's minimum pension contribution is 8% of monthly emoluments and the employer's is 10%. If Ibrahim's monthly emoluments are N320,000, how much should be deducted from his pay each month as his own contribution?
questions.explanation: The employee's share = 8% x 320,000 = N25,600. Option C applies the employer's 10% rate, and option D is the combined 18% paid by both parties. Option B is only the 2% difference between the two rates.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, an employer must contribute at least 10% of monthly emoluments and the employee at least 8%. An employee's monthly emoluments are N180,000. What is the employer's minimum contribution for a full year of 12 months?
questions.explanation: Annual employer contribution = 10% x 180,000 x 12 = N216,000. Option A is only one month's contribution, option C uses the combined 18% rate, and option B uses the employee's 8% rate.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Chioma's monthly pay is: basic salary N200,000, housing allowance N80,000, transport allowance N40,000 and meal allowance N30,000. Her contract defines pensionable emoluments as basic salary plus housing and transport allowances. Taking the minimum rates of 10% (employer) and 8% (employee) under the Pension Reform Act 2014, what is the total monthly pension contribution?
questions.explanation: Pensionable emoluments = 200,000 + 80,000 + 40,000 = N320,000, and total contribution = 18% x 320,000 = N57,600. Option B wrongly includes the meal allowance (18% of N350,000), and option D applies 18% to basic salary alone. Option C is only the employer's 10%.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, an employer that chooses to bear the full cost of pension contributions (so the employee contributes nothing) must contribute at least 20% of monthly emoluments. If an employee's monthly emoluments are N150,000, what is the employer's minimum monthly contribution under this option?
questions.explanation: When the employer bears the whole cost, the minimum is 20% of emoluments: 0.20 x 150,000 = N30,000. Option A uses the normal combined rate of 18%, while options D and C are the ordinary 10% employer and 8% employee shares.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, an employer must keep a group life insurance policy for each employee worth at least three times the employee's annual emolument. If an employee's annual emolument is N3,600,000, what is the minimum cover?
questions.explanation: Minimum cover = 3 x annual emolument = 3 x 3,600,000 = N10,800,000. Option C is only one year's emolument, option D divides by 3 instead of multiplying, and option A treats the cover as three months' pay.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014 the minimum contributions are 10% (employer) and 8% (employee) of monthly emoluments, and an employee may also make voluntary contributions. Yusuf earns monthly emoluments of N300,000 and also pays a voluntary contribution of N20,000 a month. How much goes into his retirement savings account each month in total?
questions.explanation: Mandatory contributions = 18% x 300,000 = N54,000, and adding the voluntary N20,000 gives N74,000. Option B leaves out the voluntary contribution. Option C adds the voluntary amount to the employee's 8% only, and option A adds it to the employer's 10% only.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A defined benefit (final salary) pension scheme pays an annual pension of 1/60 of final annual salary for each year of service. Mr Bello retires after 30 years of service. His final annual salary is N4,800,000 and his career-average salary is N3,600,000. What is his annual pension?
questions.explanation: Annual pension = (30 / 60) x 4,800,000 = N2,400,000. Option D wrongly uses the career-average salary instead of final salary, option C forgets to multiply by the 30 years of service, and option A is the monthly pension rather than the annual figure.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Under a defined contribution plan, N600,000 is paid into a member's account at the END of each year for 3 years. The account earns 10% per annum compounded annually. To the nearest naira, what is the account balance immediately after the third payment?
questions.explanation: This is an ordinary annuity: FV = 600,000 x [(1.1)^3 - 1] / 0.1 = 600,000 x 3.31 = N1,986,000. Option D ignores interest, and option A treats the payments as an annuity due (made at the start of each year). Option B uses simple instead of compound interest.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: An investment vehicle managed by finance professionals that lets individuals own a fraction of a large, diversified portfolio and share proportionally in its gains, losses or income is a:
questions.explanation: A mutual fund pools money from many investors to buy a spread of stocks, bonds and money market instruments, and each investor shares in the results in proportion to his holding. Option B manages retirement savings accounts rather than a fund open to all investors, option D is a type of pension promise, and option A is a single short-term government security.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Mutual funds are commonly categorised by all of the following EXCEPT:

options.c: The number of unit holders in the fund

questions.explanation: Mutual funds are grouped by how risky they are, what assets they hold and what they aim to achieve, which gives types such as money market, bond, equity and balanced funds. The number of people holding units does not define the type of fund. Options B, D and A are all standard bases of classification.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A low-risk, highly liquid mutual fund that invests in short-term securities such as treasury bills and commercial paper is a:
questions.explanation: A money market fund holds short-term instruments like treasury bills and commercial paper, so it is low risk and highly liquid. Option A invests mainly in company shares and is high risk. Option C mixes equity and bonds, and option D focuses on dollar-denominated assets.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Bisi wants somewhere to keep her emergency savings where the capital is well protected and she can withdraw quickly. Which type of mutual fund best suits her?
questions.explanation: A money market fund is low risk and highly liquid, which makes it ideal for preserving capital and holding emergency funds. Option C is high risk, so its value can fall just when she needs the money. Option B is not a mutual fund and is usually closed to ordinary investors, and option D carries medium risk because of its equity portion.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A mutual fund that invests in government and corporate debt to generate steady interest income, with low to moderate risk, is a:
questions.explanation: A fixed income or bond fund buys government and corporate debt and aims for steady interest income. Option A buys company shares, option B buys only short-term instruments, and option C avoids interest-bearing instruments altogether.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which type of mutual fund is described as high risk, high reward, because it focuses primarily on company stocks?
questions.explanation: An equity fund invests mainly in company shares, whose prices can rise or fall sharply, so it offers high potential reward with high risk. Options C and B hold debt instruments and are low or low-to-moderate risk. Option A mixes equity with bonds, giving medium risk.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A medium-risk mutual fund that combines a mixture of equities and bonds for balanced growth and risk protection is a:
questions.explanation: A balanced or hybrid fund holds both shares and bonds, so it seeks growth from equities while bonds cushion the risk. Option D is almost all shares, option A holds short-term instruments only, and option B is defined by its currency, not by an equity-bond mix.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Emeka is worried that the naira will keep depreciating and wants a mutual fund that protects the value of his savings. Which fund focuses on dollar-denominated assets for this purpose?
questions.explanation: A foreign currency fund invests in dollar-denominated assets, so its value holds up when the local currency loses value. Options D and A usually hold naira instruments and so remain exposed to depreciation. Option B is defined by its ethical rules, not by its currency.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Alhaji Musa wants to invest through a mutual fund but, for religious reasons, he will not hold interest-bearing instruments or invest in prohibited sectors. Which fund is designed for him?
questions.explanation: A halal or sharia-compliant fund is an ethically focused fund that avoids interest-bearing instruments and prohibited sectors. Options D and A earn mainly interest, which he wants to avoid. Option C is not a mutual fund and uses high-risk strategies with no such ethical restriction.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Arrange these mutual funds from LOWEST to HIGHEST risk: equity fund, money market fund, balanced fund.

options.a: Money market fund, equity fund, balanced fund
options.b: Equity fund, balanced fund, money market fund
options.c: Money market fund, balanced fund, equity fund
options.d: Balanced fund, money market fund, equity fund

questions.explanation: Money market funds are low risk, balanced funds are medium risk because they mix bonds with shares, and equity funds are high risk. Option B reverses the order. Options D and A misplace the balanced fund, which sits between the other two.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a way in which a mutual fund generates income for its investors?

options.a: Collecting fixed fees from the fund's own unit holders
options.b: Appreciation in the value of the shares it holds
options.c: Capital gains on securities sold at a profit
options.d: Dividend and interest income on its investments

questions.explanation: Fees charged to unit holders are a cost to investors and an income to the fund manager, not a return earned for investors. A mutual fund earns for its investors through dividends and interest (D), capital gains (C) and appreciation of the shares it holds (B).

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes an open-end fund from a closed-end fund?

options.a: An open-end fund creates and redeems units continuously at NAV; a closed-end fund's units trade on an exchange
options.b: An open-end fund's units trade only on a stock exchange; a closed-end fund redeems units at NAV daily
options.c: An open-end fund has a fixed number of units; a closed-end fund issues new units on demand
options.d: An open-end fund is restricted to wealthy investors; a closed-end fund is open to the public

questions.explanation: An open-end fund keeps issuing new units and buying them back from investors at a price based on net asset value. A closed-end fund issues a fixed number of units, which are then listed and traded on the exchange at market prices. Options B and C reverse the two, and option D confuses fund structure with who may invest.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Ngozi holds units in a fund that issued a fixed number of units at its launch. To sell, she must go through a stockbroker and accept the price on the stock exchange, which may differ from the fund's net asset value. Her fund is:
questions.explanation: A closed-end fund does not create or redeem units after the offer, so investors buy and sell its units on the exchange through a stockbroker at market-determined prices. Option B would buy her units back directly at NAV. Option C is a pension plan, and option D is usually an open-end fund that redeems units directly.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: For a mutual fund, (total assets - total liabilities) / number of units outstanding measures the fund's:
questions.explanation: Net asset value (NAV) is the fund's assets minus its liabilities, and dividing by the units in issue gives NAV per unit, the price at which an open-end fund issues and redeems units. Option D compares annual expenses with net assets, option A is a sales charge on purchases, and option C compares the change in value over a period with the starting value.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: In a Nigerian unit trust, the agreement between the fund manager and the trustee that sets out the parties' rights, responsibilities and the fund's investment objectives is the:
questions.explanation: A unit trust is set up under a trust deed between the fund manager and the trustee, which sets out rights, duties and investment objectives. Option D is an offer document for investors, option A is a pension account, and option B is not the founding agreement of a unit trust.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: In Nigeria, collective investment schemes such as unit trusts are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission under which current law?
questions.explanation: The Investments and Securities Act 2025, signed in March 2025, repealed the 2007 Act and is now the law under which the SEC regulates the capital market, including collective investment schemes. Option D is the repealed earlier Act. Options A and B are pension laws, which are administered by the National Pension Commission.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A sales charge deducted from an investor's money at the time units in a mutual fund are BOUGHT is called a:
questions.explanation: A front-end load is a sales charge taken when the investor buys, so less of the money is actually invested in units. Option B is charged when units are sold or redeemed. Options D and A are ongoing charges for managing the fund and for beating a target return, not a charge at purchase.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A mutual fund's total annual operating expenses expressed as a percentage of its average net assets is the:
questions.explanation: The expense ratio = annual operating expenses / average net assets, showing what share of the fund is used up each year in running costs. Option B is the fund's value per unit, option A is a one-off charge on purchase, and option D compares a closed-end fund's market price with its NAV.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A mutual fund has total assets of N520 million and total liabilities of N20 million. It has 40 million units outstanding. What is its net asset value (NAV) per unit?
questions.explanation: NAV per unit = (total assets - liabilities) / units = (520m - 20m) / 40m = N12.50. Option D ignores the liabilities (520 / 40), option B deducts the liabilities twice, and option A divides units by net assets, turning the formula upside down.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A unit trust holds securities with a market value of N85 million and cash of N5 million. It owes management fees of N2 million and has other liabilities of N3 million. There are 10 million units in issue. What is the NAV per unit?
questions.explanation: Total assets = 85m + 5m = N90m; liabilities = 2m + 3m = N5m; NAV per unit = (90m - 5m) / 10m = N8.50. Option B ignores the liabilities, option C leaves out the cash, and option D deducts only the fees owed.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Femi invests N1,000,000 in an open-end fund whose NAV is N20.00 per unit. The fund charges a front-end load of 5% of the amount invested, and the rest buys units at NAV. How many units does he receive?
questions.explanation: Load = 5% x 1,000,000 = N50,000, so N950,000 buys units: 950,000 / 20 = 47,500 units. Option C ignores the load, option B treats the load as a percentage of the net amount (1,000,000 / 1.05 / 20), and option D adds the load instead of deducting it.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A mutual fund's NAV is N19.00 per unit and it charges a front-end load of 5% of the offer (purchase) price, so that offer price = NAV / (1 - load). What is the offer price per unit?
questions.explanation: Offer price = 19.00 / (1 - 0.05) = 19.00 / 0.95 = N20.00, and the 5% load (N1.00) is 5% of that offer price. Option C adds 5% of NAV instead, option B deducts the load from NAV, and option D ignores the load.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Kemi redeems 10,000 units of an open-end fund at an NAV of N15.00 per unit. The fund charges a back-end load of 2% of the redemption value. How much does she receive?
questions.explanation: Redemption value = 10,000 x 15.00 = N150,000; the 2% back-end load is N3,000, so she receives N147,000. Option D forgets the load, option C adds it instead of deducting it, and option A is just the load itself.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: An equity fund's NAV per unit rose from N10.00 at the start of the year to N10.80 at the end, and it paid income distributions of N0.40 per unit during the year. Taking return = (change in NAV + distributions) / opening NAV, what was the fund's return for the year?
questions.explanation: Return = (10.80 - 10.00 + 0.40) / 10.00 = 1.20 / 10.00 = 12%. Option C ignores the distributions, and option D counts only the distributions. Option A divides by the closing NAV instead of the opening NAV.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A balanced fund's NAV per unit fell from N16.00 to N14.40 over the year, and it paid distributions of N0.32 per unit. Taking return = (change in NAV + distributions) / opening NAV, what was its return?
questions.explanation: Return = (14.40 - 16.00 + 0.32) / 16.00 = -1.28 / 16.00 = -8%. Option C ignores the distributions, option A gets the sign wrong, and option B divides by the closing NAV of N14.40.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A mutual fund had total annual operating expenses of N36 million and average net assets of N2.4 billion. Taking expense ratio = annual expenses / average net assets, what is its expense ratio?
questions.explanation: Expense ratio = 36m / 2,400m = 0.015 = 1.5%. Options C and A come from misplacing the decimal point (millions versus billions), and option D just quotes the expense figure as a percentage without dividing.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A fund earned a gross return of 14% on its investments for the year, and its expense ratio is 1.75%. Taking the investors' net return as gross return minus expense ratio, what was the net return?
questions.explanation: Net return = 14% - 1.75% = 12.25%, since expenses are taken out of the fund before investors share the return. Option A adds the expenses instead of deducting them, option D multiplies 14% by (1 - 0.0175), which is not the stated method, and option C is only the expense ratio.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A closed-end fund has a NAV of N25.00 per unit but its units are trading on the stock exchange at N22.50. Measuring the premium or discount as (market price - NAV) / NAV, the units are trading at:
questions.explanation: (22.50 - 25.00) / 25.00 = -0.10, so the units sell at a 10% discount to NAV. Option C gets the direction wrong, since a price below NAV is a discount. Options D and B divide by the market price instead of NAV.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Shade owns 25,000 of the 2,000,000 units in issue of a mutual fund. The fund distributes income of N8,000,000 to unit holders in proportion to their holdings. How much does Shade receive?
questions.explanation: Shade's share = (25,000 / 2,000,000) x 8,000,000 = 0.0125 x 8,000,000 = N100,000, because each unit holder shares proportionally in the fund's income. Options A and B come from misplacing the decimal point, and option C divides the income by her units instead of using her proportion.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A balanced fund invests 60% of its assets in equities expected to return 20% and 40% in bonds expected to return 12%. What is the fund's expected return as a weighted average?
questions.explanation: Expected return = (0.6 x 20%) + (0.4 x 12%) = 12% + 4.8% = 16.8%. Option B is a simple average that ignores the weights, option A swaps the weights, and option D adds the two returns together.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A private, actively managed investment pool that uses high-risk, flexible strategies to generate high returns, is loosely regulated and is typically restricted to high net worth accredited investors and institutions, is a:
questions.explanation: A hedge fund is a private, loosely regulated pool using high-risk, flexible strategies, open mainly to wealthy accredited investors and institutions. Option B is tightly regulated and open to the public, and option C is a low-risk type of mutual fund. Option A exists to provide retirement income for workers.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: The term "hedge" in hedge fund comes from the practice of:

options.a: Limiting membership to workers of one employer or union
options.b: Investing only in government treasury bills to avoid all risk
options.c: Offsetting potential losses in the core portfolio by taking inverse or protective positions
options.d: Guaranteeing investors a fixed return regardless of performance

questions.explanation: Hedging means protecting a position against loss by taking an opposite (inverse) or protective position, and hedge funds took their name from doing this. Option B describes a money market approach, option D is something hedge funds do not offer, and option A describes an occupational pension fund.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which of the following correctly compares mutual funds and hedge funds?

options.a: Mutual funds are tightly regulated and open to the public; hedge funds are loosely regulated and restricted
options.b: Both are loosely regulated and open to anyone with any amount of money
options.c: Both are tightly regulated and open only to institutional investors
options.d: Mutual funds are loosely regulated; hedge funds are tightly regulated and open to the public

questions.explanation: Mutual funds are tightly regulated and open to the general public, while hedge funds are loosely regulated and usually restricted to high net worth accredited investors and institutions. Option D reverses the two, and options C and B wrongly treat the two types of fund as the same.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a hedge fund?

options.b: It is open to the general public and tightly regulated
options.c: It pools capital from multiple investors
options.d: It is overseen by a professional fund manager

questions.explanation: Being open to the general public and tightly regulated describes a mutual fund, not a hedge fund. Hedge funds do use high-risk, flexible strategies (A), are overseen by a professional fund manager (D) and pool capital from several investors (C).

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Dayo, a first-year student with N50,000 of savings, wants professional management and a share in a diversified portfolio. Which investment vehicle is open to him?
questions.explanation: Mutual funds are open to the general public and let small investors own a fraction of a large, professionally managed portfolio. Option B is usually restricted to high net worth accredited investors and institutions. Option C is an employer pension promise, and option A is an institution that holds pension assets, not an investment he can buy.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: A hedge fund charges a management fee of 2% of assets under management plus a performance fee of 20% of the year's investment profit. Its assets under management are N1 billion and its profit for the year is N150 million. What are the total fees for the year?
questions.explanation: Management fee = 2% x 1,000m = N20m; performance fee = 20% x 150m = N30m; total = N50m. Options D and A give only one of the two fees. Option C wrongly deducts the management fee from profit before taking the performance fee, which is not the stated method.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: In the money management industry, the party that makes the investment decisions for a fund on behalf of its investors is the:
questions.explanation: The fund manager (asset manager) decides what to buy and sell for the fund on behalf of the unit holders. Option B keeps the fund's assets in safe custody, option C watches over the manager on behalf of investors under the trust deed, and option D keeps the register of unit holders.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: In a unit trust, the party whose main role is to protect the unit holders by holding the trust on their behalf and ensuring the fund manager follows the trust deed is the:
questions.explanation: The trustee is party to the trust deed and acts for the unit holders, checking that the fund manager keeps to the deed's terms and investment objectives. Option A is the party being supervised, option D only executes trades on the exchange, and option B belongs to the pension system.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Why are pension assets in Nigeria held by a pension fund custodian, separate from the pension fund administrator that invests them?

options.a: To keep contributors' assets safe and apart from the administrator's own assets
options.b: To guarantee contributors a fixed pension regardless of returns
options.c: To allow the administrator to use the assets as its working capital
options.d: To let the custodian choose the investments instead of the administrator

questions.explanation: The Pension Reform Act 2014 requires pension funds and assets to be kept separate from the operating company's assets and held with a custodian, so contributors' money is protected if the administrator gets into trouble. Option C is exactly what the separation prevents. Option D is wrong because the custodian acts on the administrator's instructions, and option B confuses custody with a defined benefit promise.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of investing through a mutual fund?

options.b: A guaranteed return that can never fall below the amount invested
options.d: Ownership of a fraction of a large portfolio with a small sum

questions.explanation: A mutual fund shares its gains AND losses with investors, so returns are not guaranteed and the value of units can fall. Professional management (C), diversification (A) and the ability to own part of a large portfolio with little money (D) are genuine advantages of mutual funds.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which of the following is a risk that an investor in an equity mutual fund must accept?

options.a: Units can never be sold or redeemed once bought
options.b: The fund cannot hold more than one company's shares
options.c: The fund manager may keep all the gains and pass on only losses
options.d: The value of units can fall when the shares in the portfolio fall

questions.explanation: Because investors share proportionally in the fund's losses as well as its gains, a fall in share prices reduces the value of their units; equity funds are high-risk for this reason. Option C is wrong because gains are shared proportionally too. Option A is false for both open-end and closed-end funds, and option B contradicts the diversified nature of a mutual fund.

questions.topic: Pension Funds, Mutual Funds and the Money Management Industry
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a type of mutual fund?
questions.explanation: A defined benefit arrangement is a type of pension plan that promises a set payout, not a mutual fund. Money market funds (A), fixed income funds (D) and halal or sharia-compliant funds (B) are all types of mutual fund classified by risk, assets and objective.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A bond is:

options.b: A debt instrument issued by a borrower

questions.explanation: A bond is a debt instrument: the issuer borrows money from investors and promises to pay interest and repay the principal at maturity. Options A and C describe shares (equity), which give ownership rather than a loan, and D describes a commodity, not a security.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A debt instrument that pays interest and is redeemable at a future date is a:
questions.explanation: A bond is a debt instrument: the issuer borrows money, pays interest over the life of the bond and repays the principal on the redemption date. Stock (B) represents ownership, not debt. A mutual fund (C) is a pooled investment, and a derivative (D) gets its value from another asset.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A bond has a face value of N1,000, pays an annual coupon of 8% and matures in 3 years. If the market yield is 10% per annum, what is its current market price, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Po = 80 x [1 - (1.10)^-3] / 0.10 + 1,000 / (1.10)^3 = 198.95 + 751.31 = N950.26. Option C values only the face value and forgets the coupons. Option D discounts at the coupon rate instead of the market yield, and B adds the coupons without discounting them.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Ikeja Holdings Plc has a 4-year bond with a face value of N1,000 and a 12% annual coupon. Investors now require a yield of 10% per annum. What is the bond's market value, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Coupon = 12% x 1,000 = N120, so Po = 120 x [1 - (1.10)^-4] / 0.10 + 1,000 / (1.10)^4 = 380.38 + 683.01 = N1,063.40, a premium because the coupon beats the yield. Option C swaps the coupon rate and the yield, B counts only the face value, and A adds all cash flows without discounting.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A 5-year bond with a face value of N1,000 pays a 10% annual coupon. If the market yield is also 10% per annum, what is the price of the bond, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: When the coupon rate equals the market yield, the bond sells at par: 100 x 3.7908 + 1,000 x 0.6209 = 379.08 + 620.92 = N1,000. Option A is only the present value of the face value and D is only the present value of the coupons. Option C ignores discounting completely.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A bond with a face value of N5,000 pays 9% interest once a year and matures in 2 years. The required yield is 12% per annum. What is the bond's value, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Annual interest = 9% x 5,000 = N450. Po = 450/1.12 + (450 + 5,000)/(1.12)^2 = 401.79 + 4,344.71 = N4,746.49. Option A swaps the coupon rate and the yield, C ignores the interest payments, and D adds the interest without discounting it.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A 3-year bond with a par value of N1,000 carries a 14% annual coupon. The market yield on similar bonds is 11% per annum. Calculate the bond's price to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Po = 140 x [1 - (1.11)^-3] / 0.11 + 1,000 / (1.11)^3 = 342.12 + 731.19 = N1,073.31. Option A wrongly uses 11% as the coupon and 14% as the yield. Option B adds only one year's coupon, undiscounted, to the PV of the face value, and C assumes the bond sells at par even though the coupon and yield differ.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: An FGN bond has a face value of N100, a 13% annual coupon and 5 years to maturity. If the market yield is 15% per annum, what is its price, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Po = 13 x [1 - (1.15)^-5] / 0.15 + 100 / (1.15)^5 = 43.58 + 49.72 = N93.30, below par because the yield is above the coupon. Option A swaps the two rates, while B and C each give only one part of the price (face value only or coupons only).

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A 2-year bond with a face value of N1,000 pays a 12% annual coupon. If the market yield is 9% per annum, by how much does its price exceed its face value (the premium), to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Price = 120/1.09 + 1,120/(1.09)^2 = 110.09 + 942.68 = N1,052.77, so the premium is 1,052.77 - 1,000 = N52.77. Option A is the discount that would arise if the two rates were swapped. Option D is the undiscounted extra coupon (3% x 1,000 x 2), and B is one year's extra coupon only.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A zero-coupon bond will pay N10,000 at maturity in 3 years and pays no interest before then. If investors require 12% per annum compounded annually, what is its price today, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: A zero-coupon bond's price is just the present value of its face value: 10,000 / (1.12)^3 = 10,000 / 1.404928 = N7,117.80. Option D uses simple discounting (1 + 0.12 x 3), C simply deducts 36% from the face value, and A uses 2 periods instead of 3.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Lekki Infrastructure issues a 4-year zero-coupon bond with a face value of N1,000. With a market yield of 15% per annum (annual compounding), at what price should it sell, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Price = 1,000 / (1.15)^4 = 1,000 / 1.74901 = N571.75, because the only cash flow is the face value at maturity. Option B uses simple interest (1 + 0.15 x 4), A discounts for only 3 years, and C wrongly multiplies by (0.85)^4 instead of dividing by (1.15)^4.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A zero-coupon bond with a face value of N1,000 matures in 3 years. The market yield is 10% per annum compounded semi-annually. What is the bond's price, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: With semi-annual compounding, the periodic rate is 10%/2 = 5% and there are 3 x 2 = 6 periods, so Po = 1,000 / (1.05)^6 = N746.22. Option D uses annual compounding, C doubles the periods but forgets to halve the rate, and A halves the rate but forgets to double the periods.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A 6-year bond with a face value of N1,000 pays an 11% annual coupon, and the market yield is 13% per annum. What is the present value of the coupon payments alone, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: The coupons form an ordinary annuity: 110 x [1 - (1.13)^-6] / 0.13 = 110 x 3.99755 = N439.73. Option A adds the coupons without discounting, B is the present value of the face value rather than the coupons, and C discounts at the coupon rate instead of the market yield.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A bond with a face value of N2,000 matures in 5 years. Using a market yield of 14% per annum, what is the present value of the face value (PT) that will be repaid at maturity, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: PV of the face value = PT / (1 + Kd)^n = 2,000 / (1.14)^5 = 2,000 / 1.925415 = N1,038.74. Option B uses simple interest (1 + 0.14 x 5), C wrongly applies the annuity factor to a single lump sum, and A uses 4 years instead of 5.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A bond with a face value of N5,000 has a coupon rate of 7.5% per annum, paid semi-annually. How much interest does the holder receive on each payment date?
questions.explanation: Annual interest = 7.5% x 5,000 = N375, and with two payments a year each payment is 375 / 2 = N187.50. Option B is the full annual coupon, A divides by four as if payments were quarterly, and D doubles the annual coupon instead of halving it.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A 4-year bond with a face value of N1,000 and a 10% annual coupon is currently priced at par because the market yield is 10%. If the market yield rises to 12% per annum, by how much does the price fall, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: At 12% the price becomes 100 x 3.03735 + 1,000 x 0.63552 = N939.25, a fall of 1,000 - 939.25 = N60.75. Option B is just 2% of face value for one year, A is 2% of face value times 4 years without discounting, and C is the rise in price that a fall to 8% would cause.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A 4-year, 10% annual coupon bond with a face value of N1,000 was bought at par. Market yields then fall to 8% per annum. What is the bond's new price, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Po = 100 x [1 - (1.08)^-4] / 0.08 + 1,000 / (1.08)^4 = 331.21 + 735.03 = N1,066.24, so the price rises as the yield falls. Option A is the price at 12%, which wrongly moves the price down. Option C counts only one undiscounted coupon, and D simply adds 8% to the face value.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Bond X (2 years) and Bond Y (6 years) both have a face value of N1,000, a 10% annual coupon and are priced at par. If the market yield rises to 12% per annum, how much MORE does Bond Y's price fall than Bond X's, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Bond X falls to N966.20 (a drop of 33.80) and Bond Y falls to N917.77 (a drop of 82.23), so Y falls 82.23 - 33.80 = N48.43 more. This shows longer-maturity bonds carry more interest rate risk. Options C and A are each bond's own price drop rather than the difference, and D wrongly assumes maturity makes no difference.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A 3-year bond with a face value of N1,000 pays a 12% coupon semi-annually. The market yield is 10% per annum compounded semi-annually. What is the bond's price, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Use 60 per half-year, a periodic rate of 5% and 6 periods: Po = 60 x [1 - (1.05)^-6] / 0.05 + 1,000 / (1.05)^6 = 304.54 + 746.22 = N1,050.76. Option B doubles the periods but forgets to halve the rate (the classic error), D treats the bond as annual, and A halves the rate but uses only 3 periods.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A bond with a face value of N1,000 pays an 8% coupon in two equal half-yearly instalments and matures in 2 years. The required yield is 12% per annum compounded semi-annually. Find the price to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Half-yearly coupon = N40, periodic rate = 6%, periods = 4: Po = 40 x 3.46511 + 1,000 / (1.06)^4 = 138.60 + 792.09 = N930.70. Option A forgets to halve the 12% rate, B treats coupons as annual, and D uses the full annual coupon of 80 every half-year.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Ogun State Government issues a 5-year bond with a par value of N1,000 that pays N50 every six months. If the market rate is 12% compounded semi-annually, what is the bond's value, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Periodic rate = 12%/2 = 6% and periods = 5 x 2 = 10, so Po = 50 x 7.36009 + 1,000 / (1.06)^10 = 368.00 + 558.39 = N926.40. Option C uses 12% per half-year (forgetting to halve the rate), A uses 5 annual periods at 12% with only N50 a year, and B wrongly assumes par even though the N50 half-yearly coupon (10% a year) is below the 12% yield.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A 2-year bond with a face value of N5,000 pays a 10% coupon semi-annually. The market yield is 8% per annum compounded semi-annually. What is its price, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Coupon per half-year = 5,000 x 10% / 2 = N250, periodic rate = 4%, periods = 4: Po = 250 x 3.62990 + 5,000 / (1.04)^4 = 907.47 + 4,274.02 = N5,181.49. Option B treats the bond as paying annually, C forgets to halve the 8% yield, and A assumes par although the coupon exceeds the yield.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Taking current yield as annual coupon / current market price, what is the current yield of a N1,000 face value bond with a 9% annual coupon that trades at N900?
questions.explanation: Current yield = 90 / 900 = 0.10, that is 10.00%. Option D is the coupon rate, which uses face value instead of market price. Option C multiplies 9% by 0.9, and B inverts the relationship (1,000 / 900 - 1).

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Taking current yield as annual coupon / current market price, a N1,000 face value bond pays a 12% annual coupon and sells for N1,250. What is its current yield, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Current yield = 120 / 1,250 = 0.096, that is 9.60%, which is below the coupon rate because the bond trades at a premium. Option C is the coupon rate, which divides by face value instead of price, D multiplies the coupon rate by 1,250 / 1,000 instead of dividing, and B is the premium (250) as a percentage of face value.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A 2-year, 10% annual coupon bond with a face value of N1,000 is priced to give a market yield of 12% per annum. Taking current yield as annual coupon / market price, what is its current yield, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: First price the bond: 100/1.12 + 1,100/(1.12)^2 = N966.20. Current yield = 100 / 966.20 = 10.35%. Option B divides by face value (giving the coupon rate), C confuses current yield with the market yield used for discounting, and A uses N120 as the coupon.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: An investor buys a call option on Dangote Cement shares with a strike price of N500 for a premium of N30 per share. At expiry the share price is N580. What is the buyer's profit per share? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: The call is exercised: payoff = 580 - 500 = N80, and profit = payoff - premium = 80 - 30 = N50. Option C is the payoff before deducting the premium, D adds the premium instead of deducting it, and A is the loss only if the option expired unused.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Halima buys a put option with a strike price of N200 for a premium of N15 per share. At expiry the share price is N160. What is her profit per share? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: A put pays strike - spot: 200 - 160 = N40, and profit = 40 - 15 = N25. Option B forgets to deduct the premium, A adds the premium, and C assumes the put is worthless even though the share price is below the strike.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A call option has a strike price of N500 and cost a premium of N30 per share. At expiry the share price is N480. What is the buyer's profit or loss per share? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: With the share price below the strike, the buyer will not exercise, so the payoff is zero and the loss equals the premium paid: -N30. Option B wrongly exercises and adds the premium to the 20 shortfall, C counts only the 20 gap, and D forgets that the premium was already paid.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Zenith Traders WROTE (sold) a put option with a strike price of N1,200 and received a premium of N50 per share. At expiry the share price is N1,100 and the buyer exercises. What is the writer's profit or loss per share? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: The writer must buy at N1,200 a share worth N1,100, losing N100, but keeps the N50 premium, so the net result is -100 + 50 = -N50. Option A is the buyer's profit, B ignores the premium received, and D treats the premium as a cost to the writer.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A writer sells a call option with a strike price of N80 for a premium of N6 per share. At expiry the share price is N75. What is the writer's profit per share? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: The share is below the strike, so the buyer does not exercise and the writer simply keeps the premium of N6, which is the most a call writer can earn. Option B is the buyer's loss, D wrongly adds the 5 gap to the premium, and A wrongly treats the N5 gap below the strike as a loss and ignores the premium.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A call option on a share has a strike price of N350 and a premium of N25. At expiry, what share price must be reached for the buyer to just break even? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: A call buyer breaks even when the payoff equals the premium: strike + premium = 350 + 25 = N375. Option B is the put break-even (strike - premium), A is the strike alone, which ignores the premium, and D double-counts the premium.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A put option on a share has a strike price of N350 and a premium of N25. Below what share price at expiry does the put buyer start making a profit? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: A put buyer breaks even at strike - premium = 350 - 25 = N325, so any price below N325 gives a profit. Option D is the call break-even, B ignores the premium, and A deducts the premium twice.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Tunde buys one call option contract covering 100 shares, with a strike price of N40 and a premium of N3 per share. At expiry the share price is N52. What is his total profit? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: Profit per share = (52 - 40) - 3 = N9, and for 100 shares that is N900. Option B forgets the premium, D adds the premium, and C is the total premium paid rather than the profit.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: An investor buys put options on 500 shares with a strike price of N60 and a premium of N4 per share. At expiry the share price is N70. What is the investor's total profit or loss? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: With the price above the strike, the put is not exercised, so the loss is the premium paid: 4 x 500 = N2,000. Option B wrongly exercises (10 x 500) without counting the premium, C nets the 10 gap against the premium, and D treats the rise as a gain to the put buyer.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A put option has a strike price of N600. At expiry the share price is N650. What is the payoff (before premium) to the put holder per share?
questions.explanation: A put pays max(strike - spot, 0) = max(600 - 650, 0) = 0, because nobody would sell at N600 a share worth N650; the holder simply lets it expire. Option B is the payoff of a call, A forgets that the holder can refuse to exercise, so payoff is never negative, and D confuses payoff with the share price.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Ada buys 10 call option contracts on MTN Nigeria shares, each covering 100 shares, at a premium of N2.50 per share. What is the maximum amount she can lose? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.

options.c: Unlimited, if the share price keeps rising

questions.explanation: An option buyer's loss is limited to the premium paid: 10 x 100 x 2.50 = N2,500. Option D covers only one contract, A covers 10 shares, and C describes the risk of an uncovered call writer, not a buyer.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: An investor owns 1,000 shares and buys put options on them with a strike price of N90 at a premium of N5 per share. At expiry the share price has fallen to N70. Counting the premium, what is the effective amount per share she receives by exercising and selling at the strike? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: Exercising the put lets her sell at N90, and after the N5 premium she effectively receives 90 - 5 = N85 per share, which is the floor the hedge guarantees. Option B ignores the premium, C is the unhedged market price, and D deducts the premium from the market price instead.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A call option has a strike price of N100 and a premium of N8. At expiry, what share price would give the buyer a profit of exactly N20 per share? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: Profit = (spot - strike) - premium, so 20 = (S - 100) - 8 and S = N128. Option C ignores the premium, D subtracts the premium instead of adding it, and B is the break-even price (strike + premium), where profit is zero.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: An investor buys a put option on 100 shares of a bank, strike price N75, premium N6 per share. At expiry the share price is N60. What is the total profit? Ignore transaction costs and the time value of money.
questions.explanation: Profit per share = (75 - 60) - 6 = N9, so total profit = 9 x 100 = N900. Option C forgets the premium, A adds it, and B treats the option as unexercised.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A Kano food processor enters a forward contract to buy 200 bags of rice in 3 months at N45,000 per bag. On the delivery date the spot price is N48,000 per bag. What is the processor's gain from the forward compared with buying at spot?
questions.explanation: The buyer pays the agreed N45,000 instead of N48,000, saving 3,000 x 200 = N600,000. Option B is the full spot cost of 200 bags, D is the gain on one bag only, and A is the seller's result, not the buyer's.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A maize farmer agrees in a forward contract to sell 50 tonnes at harvest for N300,000 per tonne. At harvest the spot price is N270,000 per tonne. How much does the farmer receive in total under the contract?
questions.explanation: A forward is binding, so the farmer delivers 50 tonnes at the agreed price: 50 x 300,000 = N15,000,000, whatever the spot price. Option D uses the spot price, A is only the gain over spot, and C wrongly adds both prices together.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A Lagos manufacturer agrees a forward contract to buy US$10,000 in 6 months at N1,500 per dollar. At maturity the spot rate is N1,560 per dollar. How much naira does the forward save the manufacturer?
questions.explanation: Without the forward the dollars would cost 10,000 x 1,560 = N15.6m; with it they cost N15.0m, a saving of 60 x 10,000 = N600,000. Option B is the saving per dollar, A is the forward cost, and D is the spot cost.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A trader holds one long futures contract covering 100 units. The settlement price moves from N2,000 to N2,040 in one day. With daily settlement, how much is credited or debited to the trader's margin account that day?
questions.explanation: A long position gains when the futures price rises: 40 x 100 = N4,000 is credited at the end of the day. Option C is what happens to the short side, D forgets to multiply by the contract size, and B is the value of the whole contract, not the day's change.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A speculator is long one futures contract of 1,000 units bought at N500. The daily settlement prices over the next three days are N510, N495 and N505. What is the net amount credited to the margin account over the three days?
questions.explanation: Daily settlements are +10,000, -15,000 and +10,000, giving a net of +N5,000, the same as (505 - 500) x 1,000. Option B is only the second day, C adds the sizes of the moves (10 + 15 + 10 = 35) x 1,000 and ignores that one was a loss, and A is the short side's result.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A trader deposits an initial margin of N50,000 and takes a short futures position on 200 units at N1,000 per unit. If losses are deducted from the margin account daily and the futures price rises to N1,180, what is the margin balance (assuming no top-ups)?
questions.explanation: A short position loses when the price rises: 180 x 200 = N36,000 loss, so the balance is 50,000 - 36,000 = N14,000. Option A treats the rise as a gain, B is the loss itself, and D forgets to multiply by 200 units.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A long futures position on 100 units has an initial margin of N20,000 and a maintenance margin of N15,000. The futures price falls by N70 per unit. If a margin call requires topping the account back up to the initial margin, how much must the trader deposit?
questions.explanation: The loss is 70 x 100 = N7,000, leaving 13,000, which is below the 15,000 maintenance level, so the account must go back to 20,000: a deposit of N7,000. Option C tops up only to the maintenance margin, A is the remaining balance, and B wrongly says no call is needed.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A speculator buys 5 futures contracts, each covering 1,000 units, at N25.00 per unit and closes them out at N27.50 per unit. What is the speculator's total profit?
questions.explanation: Profit = (27.50 - 25.00) x 1,000 x 5 = N12,500. Option B counts only one contract, A is the closing value of all contracts, and D wrongly multiplies the price gain by 50,000 units.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A bakery uses futures to fix the price of 20 tonnes of wheat at N400,000 per tonne. At settlement the spot price is N450,000 per tonne; the bakery buys at spot and receives the gain on its futures. What is its net cost of the wheat?
questions.explanation: Spot cost = 20 x 450,000 = N9,000,000, futures gain = 50,000 x 20 = N1,000,000, so net cost = N8,000,000, which is exactly the locked price. Option D ignores the hedge, A is only the futures gain, and C adds the gain instead of deducting it.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A call option has a strike price of N1,000 and the underlying share now trades at N1,150. A put on the same share has the same strike. What are the payoffs per share if both are exercised (or allowed to expire) at this price?
questions.explanation: The call pays max(1,150 - 1,000, 0) = N150, while the put pays max(1,000 - 1,150, 0) = 0, so the put holder lets it expire. Option B swaps the two, C wrongly gives the put a negative payoff, and A confuses the call payoff with the share price.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Bonds are described as 'fixed income' instruments mainly because they

options.a: promise the holder regular interest payments of a fixed amount
options.b: give the holder a fixed share of the issuer's profits
options.c: are always sold at exactly their face value
options.d: can only be sold back to the issuer at a fixed price

questions.explanation: A bond's coupon is set when it is issued, so the holder knows in advance the interest (R) to be received each period, plus the principal at maturity. Option B describes equity, whose returns depend on profits. Option D is false because bonds trade on the secondary market, and C is false because prices move above or below face value as yields change.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Bisi buys newly issued Federal Government of Nigeria bonds worth N2 million. In relation to the government, Bisi has become

options.a: a lender (creditor) to whom interest and principal are owed
options.b: the writer of an option on government revenue
options.c: a part-owner entitled to vote on government policy
options.d: a party to a futures contract with the government

questions.explanation: A bond is a loan made by the investor and owed by the borrower, here the government, so Bisi is a creditor entitled to interest and repayment of principal. Option C describes a shareholder in a company, while B and D describe derivative positions, not bond ownership.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: Governments and companies issue bonds mainly in order to

options.a: avoid paying interest on borrowed funds
options.b: hedge the price of raw materials
options.c: raise capital for operations or new projects
options.d: transfer ownership of the business to investors

questions.explanation: Bonds are a way of borrowing: issuers raise capital for operations or new projects and pay interest in return. Option D is what issuing shares does, B is the job of derivatives such as futures, and A is wrong because bondholders are paid interest.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: In the bond valuation formula Po = SUM[R / (1 + Kd)^t] + PT / (1 + Kd)^n, what does Kd represent?

options.a: The face or terminal value repaid at maturity
options.b: The market yield (required return) used to discount the bond's cash flows
options.c: The number of years to maturity
options.d: The annual fixed interest paid on the bond

questions.explanation: Kd is the yield, the rate investors require, and it is the discount rate applied to each coupon and to the face value. Option D is R, A is PT and C is n.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: In bond valuation, the symbol PT stands for

options.a: the total of all coupons over the bond's life
options.b: the face or terminal value of the bond
options.d: the current market price of the bond

questions.explanation: PT is the face (terminal) value, the principal repaid when the bond matures, and it is discounted with (1 + Kd)^n. Option D is Po, the value being calculated, C is R, and A is not a symbol in the formula at all.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: In the bond valuation formula, which symbol represents the bond's annual fixed interest payment?
questions.explanation: R is the annual fixed interest (the coupon in naira), for example 10% of a N1,000 face value gives R = N100. Po is the current market price (option D), PT is the face value (option A) and Kd is the market yield (option B).

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: The expression SUM[R / (1 + Kd)^t] + PT / (1 + Kd)^n, with t running from 1 to n, calculates

options.a: the current market price (value) of a bond
options.b: the future value of the bond's coupons at maturity
options.c: the current yield of the bond
options.d: the total interest a bondholder receives

questions.explanation: The formula discounts every coupon and the face value back to today, so it gives Po, the current market price. Option B would require compounding forward, not discounting. Option C is coupon divided by price, and D would simply be R x n with no discounting.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: When valuing a bond that pays a fixed annual coupon, the stream of coupons is most conveniently valued using

options.a: the future value of an annuity due factor
options.b: the present value of an ordinary annuity factor
options.d: the present value of a single lump sum factor applied once

questions.explanation: Equal coupons at the end of each year form an ordinary annuity, so they are valued with [1 - (1 + Kd)^-n] / Kd, then the face value is added as a separate lump sum. Option A compounds forward and assumes payments at the start, D suits only the face value, and C ignores compounding.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: What happens to the price of an existing fixed-coupon bond when market interest rates (yields) rise?

options.b: It rises only if the bond is close to maturity
options.c: It stays the same because the coupon is fixed

questions.explanation: Price and yield move in opposite directions: a higher yield in the denominator reduces the present value of the fixed coupons and face value. Option A gets the direction wrong, C confuses a fixed coupon with a fixed price, and B has no basis because rising yields push prices down at every maturity.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A bond whose market yield is HIGHER than its coupon rate will sell

options.a: at a premium, above its face value
options.b: at a discount, below its face value
options.c: at a price equal to its total coupons

questions.explanation: If investors require more than the coupon pays, they will only buy at a lower price, so the bond sells at a discount, as when a 10% coupon bond priced at 12% is worth about N927.88 per N1,000. Option A applies when the yield is below the coupon, and D applies when they are equal. Option C has no basis.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
questions.question: A bond is trading at a premium (above its face value). This means that

options.a: its coupon rate is higher than the current market yield
options.c: its coupon rate is lower than the current market yield
options.d: its coupon rate equals the current market yield

questions.explanation: A premium arises when the bond pays more interest than investors currently require, so they bid the price above par. Option C produces a discount, D produces a price at par, and B is wrong because zero-coupon bonds always sell below face value when yields are positive.

questions.topic: Bonds, Interest Rates, Forwards, Futures and Options
